description: A cylindrical hole 7/16ths in. diam. is drilled in the head of the bolt into which the 15-in. observing rod or the foot of the traverse pole can be fitted. The bolt is protected by an iron cap or hydrant cover according to the nature of the surface. An observing pin and small circular spirit level for setting it vertical are also shown.

This type of mark set either in rock or masonry is used for marking the first order triangulation stations in France. It consists of a small cylindrical bronze bolt with grooved sides and a cross engraved on its upper face, the intersection of the cross indicating the station point.
Elliptical metal plate fixed in masonry at a first order triangulation station in France, and carries a number corresponding to the particular station point.

This mark consists of a brass disc and shank cast in one piece. The shank is ribbed so as to grip securely the material—generally rock or concrete—in which the mark is set. One such mark is set at the surface and a similar one about 3 ft. directly underneath it at every triangulation station. The station point is defined by a small dot within a 20 mm. equilateral triangle engraved on the disc.

This mark is the older form of station mark used by the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey. Its shank is split so that a wedge can be inserted. When the mark is driven into the drill-hole, the wedge causes the shank to bulge and grip firmly the surrounding material. The station point is defined by a dot enclosed in two intersecting 20-mm. equilateral triangles engraved on the disc.

This mark is the same as that used for triangulation station marks, except that the central hole or dot is here surrounded by a 2.5-cm. circle. The mark is set in a post or block of concrete, or wedged into a drill-hole in rock, after which a triangle or circle is chiselled round it. For underground station marks a similar disc is set 3 ft. below ground in a block of concrete, in rock or other suitable material.

A metal disc and shank used to facilitate the recovery of station marks, especially where these are liable to damage or disturbance. The mark is placed so that the arrow engraved thereon points to the station mark, and the horizontal distance between the station mark and the groove cut across the shaft of the arrow is recorded. Reference marks are set in concrete posts or blocks, or in rock, at distances up to 20 yd. from the station marks.

Stations of the Primary Triangulation of Canada are marked by means of circular metal bolts of the type exhibited, the bolts being embedded in concrete or leaded into rock. Both underground and surface marks are employed, and reference monuments provided to facilitate recovery of the station. The bolt consists of a 3-in. circular bronze disc, attached to a 3-in. cylindrical shank, which is corrugated and fox-wedged so that the shank expands tightly against the sides of the hole drilled to receive it when the bolt is driven in. The centre of the disc has a triangle engraved upon it, with a central hole punched to define the exact station point.

A bronze bolt with an arrow engraved upon it to indicate the direction in which the station point lies. Used as a reference mark for primary triangulation stations where station marks are in danger of disturbance or difficult to find. Typically set in outstanding rocks or concrete monuments.
A rectangular plate with two projecting shanks for fixing it into a reference monument. Used by the Geodetic Survey of Canada to mark station points where no natural rock is available.

This brass bolt forms the station mark at a geodetic station of the Survey of Egypt. It is provided with two saw-cuts intersecting at right angles, and is cemented into a concrete block in the ground. Accurately built into the concrete block is an iron cylinder filled with concrete, having gaps in the bottom so that the mark can be seen. A brass and cast iron tribrach (see Cat. No. 14) is accurately centred over the mark and cemented in the top of the pillar. Upon this tribrach the theodolite rests when sighting to the station, whilst to its centre is screwed a heliograph or lamp when sighting to the station.

This brass tribrach is built into a masonry pier and accurately centred over the concealed mark at geodetic stations in Egypt. It has three radial V-shaped grooves at angles of 120° with one another, and forms a self-centring stand for the three feet of a theodolite or signal lamp.

First Order. This bolt forms the upper reference point at a fundamental bench mark on the first order levelling lines of the Ordnance Survey. It is fixed in the top of a granite block forming a pillar 12 in. high, and is the mark for use in all ordinary circumstances, its level being recorded on the topographical maps.

First Order. This bolt forms one of the two concealed reference points at a fundamental bench mark of the Ordnance Survey. It is set in rock concrete 3 ft. below ground in a concrete recess 3 ft. square by 1 ft. 9 in. deep.
This plate is affixed to the granite pillar of a fundamental bench mark of the Ordnance Survey.
The cover is placed below ground in a fundamental bench mark chamber to protect the reference marks of the Ordnance Survey from interference or damage.

Secondary marks are fixed on lines of first order levelling. These consist of a gun-metal plate set flush with the surface of a wall, and having an identification number cast on it. The reference point, to which the published altitude corresponds, is the top of the "broad arrow." In levelling, the foot of the levelling staff is brought to the same altitude as this point with the aid of a detachable bracket and a small spirit-level.

This adjustable bracket is used for supporting the levelling staff at a secondary bench mark on the lines of the first order levelling of the Ordnance Survey. The bracket is hooked on to the bench mark, and the surface, upon which the levelling staff is placed, is made level and in agreement with the reference point by means of the adjusting screw and the spirit level.

An old type of angle iron used to support the levelling staff at an Ordnance Survey broad arrow bench mark. It has a short arm which is fitted into the horizontal groove engraved above the broad arrow, and a longer inclined supporting arm which abuts against the wall in which the mark was notched. A series of circular depressions are sunk in the upper face to receive the stud on the base of the staff, the lower level of the depressions being a horizontal plane passing through the centre line of the engraved groove.

This modern type of bracket is used to support the levelling staff at a broad arrow bench mark of the Ordnance Survey. It is broader than the adjacent earlier type, and has an adjusting screw threaded through its inclined arm and a box level mounted on its horizontal arm; the end of the screw butts against the vertical wall in which the mark is engraved, and the inclination of the upper arm can be adjusted level by turning the screw. The flat base of the metal shoe forming the end of the staff rests on a stud projecting from the top of the bracket, the top of the stud being level with the centre line of the mark when the bracket is horizontal.

This brass disc is fixed with its face flush with the building in which it is set or with its stem vertical in rock or cement. The short line in the centre is placed horizontal and serves as the reference point.

First Order. This mark is used at first-order stations of the Nivellement Général de la France. It consists of a metal bolt having a grooved shank and a rectangular plate head with a recess to receive a plate, on which the height of the station point is printed. The reference point is the top of a spherical boss on a horizontal platform which projects from the plate.

A metal bolt with a grooved shank and cylindrical head; on the top of the curved surface of the head is a small spherical boss, the top of which is the reference point. The height of this point is printed on a plate embedded in the cylindrical head.

First Order mark consisting of an iron bolt with a hexagonal head. It is cemented into a vertical wall or solid rock. The point of reference is the top of a bronze hemispherical stud on the top of the upper face of the head.
Second Order. This mark is similar to the adjacent first order bench mark, except that it has a cylindrical head, of which the highest point is the reference point.

Bronze tablets of this type are used by the Geodetic Survey of Canada to mark the station points of the Precise Levelling Network. The tablet is a circular disc provided with a corrugated, fox-wedged shank for fixing it into rock or concrete. The centre of the disc is engraved with a cross, and a number can be stamped on it with a die for reference to the record book, which contains the particulars of the corresponding station.

These two photographs illustrate the construction of quadripod triangulation beacons at Ado Rock and Awba Hill stations during the survey of Southern Nigeria, 1910–12. The beacons are formed of tree-trunks and branches built up into a four-sided pyramid, the upper part of which is roofed with brushwood to form a prominent land-mark, and at the same time to protect the surveying instruments when taking bearings from the station. A pole carrying at its upper end a white flag is fixed to the top of the beacon to render it more conspicuous. The right hand photograph shows the framework of the beacon built up, but the roof not yet added. The left hand photograph shows a completed beacon, with a heliograph, theodolite and plane table standing beneath it. The ground in the vicinity has been carefully cleared of obstacles to view.

The telescope is mounted on a circle capable of rotation about a horizontal axis, and can itself revolve about the centre of the circle. This circle has no divisions and is only for giving a slow motion to the telescope by means of a screw. Through a sleeve on the telescope passes a brass rod carrying a mirror perpendicular to it; the distances of the mirror and the sleeve from the axis of rotation of the telescope being equal. In order to send a ray of sunlight in a specified direction, the instrument is set up so that the mark is in the centre of the field when the axis of the telescope is normal to the plane of the mirror. If, then, the telescope is directed to the sun and follows it continuously, the mirror will reflect its light on to the mark.

A heliotrope for use in triangulation. For use the telescope was directed on the triangulation mark, the small central mirror being turned parallel to the axis of the telescope. Then the double-mirror was turned until its axis was at right angles to a plane containing the sun, the instrument and the distant mark. This is facilitated by the disc beside the mirror, upon which its shadow is a fine line only, the mirror is in position. Lastly, the double mirror is rotated until the sun’s image as reflected by the central mirror is seen in the telescope, when the outer mirror reflects the sun’s light on to the distant mark.

This instrument, sometimes also called a heliostat, was used for reflecting the sun’s rays to an observing station. Three sizes were in use by the Ordnance Survey in the principal triangulation; the largest were rectangular and measured 20 in. by 16 in., the other two were circular and were 12 in. and 5 in. diam. respectively. In each case the mirror, having been centred over the triangulation mark, was moved by hand so as to follow the sun and to reflect its light through a ring placed in the line between the heliostat, or the reflecting station, and the observing station. The ring was placed in position by means of a small theodolite.

This lamp is an acetylene projector designed by Mr. G. T. McCaw for use in trigonometrical surveys. It was first used in the measurement of an arc of meridian in Uganda, and later in the Royal Siamese Survey Department. For work by day a heliograph was attached to the front of the instrument, and projected its beam of sunlight through a hole cut in a board nailed to a post fixed from 10 to 20 ft. in front of the instrument. This was found less confusing to the native assistants in Rhodesia and Uganda than the mirrors of a self-contained heliograph such as is ordinarily employed in Army signalling.

This electric lamp is used at stations of the Primary Triangulation of Canada to mark the station point during night observations. It is visible at distances up to 130 miles. The lamp is of the type used for motor-car headlights, and has a parabolic reflector behind the bulb. It is mounted within a wooden frame which can be supported upon the box within which it is packed for travelling, and can be adjusted upon this box by means of an elevating screw. The top of the frame has metal V-s attached to support the telescope used in aligning the lamp upon the observing station. Two bulbs of different sizes are supplied with the lamp for use at smaller and larger distances respectively. They are illuminated by current supplied by a battery of dry cells. An electrically controlled time-switch can be connected in the circuit to light automatically the lamps at regular intervals.

This instrument, for registering the number of paces made by the person carrying it, resembles a watch in size, appearance and general details of construction. The "escapement" is, however, not actuated by a pendulum or balance wheel, but by a rocking lever and spring pawl which engages in a ratchet wheel. The lever is depressed by the forward movement of the wearer's leg, which stretches a connecting cord attached to the split ring at the top of the instrument. This disengages the spring pawl momentarily and permits one tooth of the ratchet wheel to slip past its point. As the motion of the observer's leg slackens the tension in the cord, a counter spring forces the lever into its former position ready for the next forward movement. The ratchet wheel thus moves one tooth at every alternate stride of the wearer, and is connected with the pinion wheel train, dials and pointers which record the steps taken. There are four such dials and pointers, for the units, hundreds, thousands and ten thousands respectively, the units dial having 50 graduations and its pointer moving over one division every alternate pace of the observer.

The cord which is attached to the observer's leg and actuates the rocking lever, is also exhibited; it passes over a small pulley wheel mounted in the head of the pedometer. The main dial in this instrument has its divisions numbered in two sets, and a pointer corresponding to each set. The outer set records the unit paces, and the inner set the tens. A second dial and pointer registers the thousands up to twelve. The units pointer moves over two divisions at a time, as it is only moved at every alternate step of the observer.

This is a late 18th century pedometer, of a construction less sensitive than the adjacent one by the same makers. The rocking lever is here attached to a pin fitting across the top of the case, and the long hook is mounted upon the same pin, so as to embrace it tightly. As the hook is swung by the motion of the person carrying the instrument, the pin rotates and causes the lever to rock. A two-pronged spring pawl is fixed to the lever at its upper end and engages the teeth of a ratchet wheel at its lower end. As the lever rocks, the pawl causes the ratchet to slip a tooth, and thus turns a pinion wheel mounted on the same axis. The pinion gears in the train of wheels which record the paces taken. As only alternate paces are recorded, the dials and pointers are arranged accordingly. Miles and decimal parts of a mile are registered on three dials, the instrument recording up to 12 miles at intervals of one thousandth of a mile. The long hook serves to suspend the pedometer from the fob so that it rests against the thigh, and thus gets the desired swing as the wearer walks.

A pedometer with a more delicate escapement, actuated by the sudden stoppage in the motion of the wearer’s body at each step. The long hook is used to suspend the instrument from the fob of the person carrying it. The escapement is effected by the withdrawal of a spring pawl, attached to one end of a rocking lever, from the teeth of a small ratchet wheel. The teeth are very fine, so that the pawl slips over four teeth at each oscillation. The lever is normally kept in the "down" position by a fairly strong spring, but the pull of this spring is considerably reduced by slightly raising the long hook projecting from the top. The lower end of this hook is fixed to a chain wound round a drum mounted on the same spindle as the rocking lever. The hook is raised when the instrument is fitted in its case by inserting a pin in a hole in the lower end of the hook, the ends of the pin resting in brackets on the top of the case. In this position, the rocking lever is just balanced, and is very sensitive to small jerks. The instrument has three dials and pointers registering miles, tenths, and thousandths of a mile. The pointer of the thousandths dial is connected to the ratchet wheel and so geared that it moves 176 times in one revolution, i.e. in one tenth of a mile. The pedometer is mounted separately from its case for exhibiting the movement mechanism.

This instrument was made about 1800 and consists of a pedometer and a watch mounted in the same case and having a common face, with separate dials and pointers. The pedometer movement is effected by the tension of a string, which is attached at one end to the wearer’s leg, and at the other to a delicately poised rocking lever controlling by its oscillations the engagement of a spring pawl in a ratchet wheel. The large pedometer dial is graduated to record every hundred double paces; there is a smaller one to register every ten double paces, and a third to record each double pace.

The movement here exhibited is of the type invented by W. Payne in 1831 and still used in modern pedometers. The escapement of the recording ratchet wheel is effected by the oscillations of a horizontal anchor-shaped pendulum, whose moment about its pivot is just more than balanced by the pressure of a control spring. The sudden jerk caused by the stoppage of the downward motion of the wearer’s body at each step is sufficient to make the pendulum oscillate. A spring pawl, fixed at one end to the pendulum arm, engages at its other end the teeth of the ratchet wheel. A counter spring pawl, pivoted in the bed of the instrument, opposes the thrust of the former with a force sufficient to damp the rotary movement of the ratchet. (This opposing spring is missing in the instru- ment shown.) The teeth of the ratchet are very fine, so that as the pendulum moves from the upper stop to the lower, the pawl passes over several teeth, the number depending upon the adjustment of the lower stop, which is threaded in a fixed block. By this adjustment, the indication of the recording pinion can be varied to correspond roughly to the length of the observer's stride. The ratchet wheel is geared to a train of pinion wheels which record the distance travelled in miles and furlongs. There is only one dial and pointer, the former graduated in miles up to twelve, with eight sub-divisions to each mile. The numbering of the main graduations is like that used in watches.

This instrument has the movement invented by W. Payne in 1831 and shown in the preceding exhibit. The movement of the horizontal pendulum is restricted by stops, the lower one being adjustable to allow approximately for the variation in the length of stride. The instrument is carried in the waistcoat pocket and kept in a vertical position by means of the spring clip attached to its ring. It has a single dial, graduated in miles and quarters up to 12 miles. Fractions of quarter-miles can be estimated by the position of the pointer between the graduations.

The Odometer, Waywiser or Perambulator has been employed since the days of the Romans for measuring distances by counting and recording the revolutions of a wheel of known circumference. It has a brass wheel of 1.5 ft. circumference geared to a registering mechanism furnished with dials and pointers which record the number of links, poles, chains, furlongs, and miles traversed. The bearings for the wheel axle are fixed to metal brackets screwed to the case containing the registering mechanism, which itself is fixed at the lower extremity of a long wooden handle. At one end of the axle is a small pinion wheel the teeth of which engage in those of a perpendicular pinion mounted on the lower end of a brass rod, which is pivoted at its lower end in the axle bearing block and kept parallel to the supporting bracket by guides. The upper end of this rod is geared to the case containing the registering mechanism. This has two pointers and dials, the outer one divided to read links and having divisions both every ten links and every pole, whilst the inner dial is graduated in miles and half furlongs up to four miles.

An improved form of the adjacent Waywiser, made by Adams. The wheel is much larger, its circumference being half a pole, and it is carefully mounted in its bearings so as to reduce friction and shake. The mechanism differs slightly from that in the Waywiser. The motion of the rotating axle of the wheel is transmitted to a perpendicular shaft running along the top to the case containing the recording mechanism by a pair of bevel wheels, and from the shaft to the recording mechanism by a worm and worm-wheel. One of the bearing forks is hinged at the top to the case containing the recording mechanism. The outer dial has a diam. of 7 in. and is graduated in yards and poles, its pointer making one revolution every furlong. An inner dial, of 5 in. diam. is graduated in furlongs and miles up to 10 miles and is read by a second index.

A measuring wheel constructed specially for use on frozen snow surface and ice. The instrument has a trailing wheel of diam. 18 in. made of steel, with an aluminium band on its rim to prevent snow from clinging to the surface and with steel pegs fitted into the rim so as to enable the wheel to roll without slipping on ice surfaces. The wheel is mounted in ball bearings upon a metal fork to which the recording mechanism is attached. The gearing is completely enclosed and the dial gives reading in geographical miles, subdivided to 25 yd. The fork is fixed to a wooden bar to which at the other end is attached a cross-head connected to the bar by a universal joint. This permits the instrument to follow the track of a sledge without partaking of its lateral movements.

The chain most generally used in England for land measurement is named after its inventor, Edmund Gunter, and was first employed about 1620. It has a length of 66 ft. made up of 100 links, so that 10 square chains equal one acre. The example shown is made of iron, with brass handles, as was formerly the custom. This type has been replaced by the chain made of steel wire, of No. 8 or No. 12 B.W.G. which stretches much less than an iron chain after use. In all Gunter’s chains, brass tellers are inserted at every 10 links, for convenience in estimating fractional lengths.

This chain, which is 66 ft. long and has 100 links, is representative of the modern land surveyor’s chain. A central swivel is fitted to obviate kinks when the chain is twisted in use. When not in use, the chain is folded up in the manner shown, and bound together with a leather strap.

A steel band preferred to a chain by many land surveyors because it is lighter and preserves its length better. It is 50 ft. long and is divided every foot, the two terminal feet being subdivided into inches. The divisions are marked by brass studs of various sizes, an oval plate being substituted for the stud at every 10 ft. and marked by perforation to show the length from the nearer end. The handles are made of brass, with swivel joints. The whole is wound up in a metal case which has a narrow slit for inserting the handle at one end. A strap is attached to the case for carrying it.

An accurately graduated steel tape of this type is extensively used for short measurements. This example is graduated throughout in millimetres. When not in use, it is wound up in the leather case as shown.
Wooden rods (Messlatten, Messtangen) similar to the pair here shown are commonly used in Germany in land-measurement, and have been in use in Würtemburg for several centuries.
interpretation: Commonly used in Germany in land-measurement, and have been in use in Würtemburg for several centuries.

description: Rods of square section with wedge-shaped metal ends. In one rod the metres are painted alternately red and white; in the other, black and white. Each rod is graduated in decimetres.
interpretation: Their length is verified before use by laying each rod on a test-bed provided with chisel-shaped stops at a known distance apart. By measuring the interval between the rod and the test-bed with a measuring wedge the length of the rod is obtained.

description: A steel measuring wedge of uniformly varying thickness is inserted between the two terminals to accurately measure the small distance between one end of a wooden measuring rod and the end of a standard. The exhibited wedge has a uniform variation in thickness of 1 mm. per 1 cm. of its length. Its length is graduated in millimetres, reading by estimation to tenth-millimetres, and thus giving the corresponding thickness to 0·01 mm., within a range of error of 0·01 mm.

description: A steel chain with 100 links, each 1 ft. long. The joints at every 10 ft. are at right angles to the remainder, which permits the chain to be folded so as to fit into a box about 14 in. by 8 in. by 8 in. for transport. Brass plates are attached at the joints to indicate 10 ft. lengths along the chain. In the rough measurement of the Hounslow Heath base, the chain appears to have been simply stretched along the ground, but in the measurement at Romney Marsh it was supported on deal coffers, 20 ft. long, resting on carefully aligned posts driven into the ground every 20 ft. along the base. Thus supported, the chain was stretched by a weight of 28 lb., the temperature being measured by thermometers laid in the coffers near the chain.
measurements: ['1 ft. long (each link)', '100 links', '14 in. by 8 in. by 8 in. (box)', '20 ft. long (coffers)', '28 lb. (weight)']
interpretation: This chain was first used by General Roy in measuring the Hounslow Heath base in 1784. Although it was only used as a preliminary to more precise measurements with both fir and glass rods, General Roy was so impressed by its accuracy that, in measuring the base of verification on Romney Marsh in 1787, he used the chain only, and discarded the wooden and glass rods.

interpretation: Used to sight between two terminal tripods upon boning rods set up at subdivision points. The movable vanes of these rods were adjusted until their index lines lay on the axis of sight of the telescope, thus ascertaining the height of the intermediate tripods. The magnifying power of the eyepiece is small, and the telescope can be focussed down to a few feet.

description: The apparatus consists of four wrought iron bars enclosed in wooden cases, supported near the ends on trestles. The chief peculiarity of the bars is the use of spring contact levers. The temperature was measured directly by thermometers whose bulbs rested in cavities in the bar. Struve estimated the mean probable error of his bases as 1 in 7,250,000. Each iron bar is 2 toises (nearly 4 m.) long, and has a square section of 3·4 cm. side. It terminates at one end in a small steel cylinder, having a slightly convex outer face. To the other end is pivoted a lever with unequal arms. On the lower arm is a polished hemisphere, pushed outwards from the bar by a weak spring. The steel cylinder of the adjacent bar makes contact with this hemisphere, and forces the longer arm of the lever to traverse a vertical graduated scale. Any slight variation in length of the bar is correspondingly magnified by the lever on the scale, and can be accurately measured. Two mercury thermometers are placed with their bulbs in recesses in each bar, and serve to measure the temperature directly. There is also a spirit level attached to determine the inclination of the bar.
interpretation: Designed by W. Struve and used by him in measuring seven bases of the principal triangulation of Russia. The apparatus is used for accurately measuring variations in length of the bars.
interpretation_source: Encyclopædia Britannica,” XI Edition, Article “ Geodesy.

description: A measuring tape made of an "invar" nickel-steel alloy, containing 35-36% nickel. The tape is just over 100 ft. long, with scales divided to read two-hundredths of a foot at each end. The National Physical Laboratory certificate of examination states its length between zero marks at each end is 100.001 ft. at 58.5° F., under a tension of 10 kg., with an accuracy of 1 in 100,000. The width of the tape is 5 mm. and its thickness 0.5 mm. It is wound upon an aluminium drum of 16 in. diameter, which can rotate upon its pivot.

interpretation: The "invar" alloy has a low coefficient of expansion (not greater than 1.0 x 10⁻⁶ per °C), discovered by Dr. C. E. Guillaume in 1896. This property is valuable for geodesy as it minimizes errors in measuring units due to temperature variations. Its low coefficient of expansion is important. "Invar" wires or tapes are used universally in measuring bases for triangulation of the first or second order, suspended under a constant tension of about 10 kg., according to Jäderin’s method.

description: This instrument was designed by Capt. G. H. Blakey, R.N. for determining the distance of a ship on the assumption that the height of its mast is known, and that the mast is perpendicular to the direction of the ship from the observer. It is merely a telescopic sighting tube having a pin-hole aperture and pairs of parallel wires set at known intervals apart near the object end of the tube. The distance of these wires from the aperture is given by the graduated scales on the telescopic tube. In using the instrument, the mast of the distant ship is viewed and the sighting tube telescoped until the mast lies exactly between a pair of wires. On reading the length of the tube, i.e. from aperture to wires, the range of the mast will be in the same ratio to this length as the mast is to the interval between the wires. As these last two lengths are known, the range is readily calculated, or can be obtained directly from the tables supplied with the instrument. Two mutually perpendicular pairs of parallel wires are fitted in the instrument exhibited, at intervals of one tenth and one twentieth of a foot respectively. A table corresponding to the former interval for lengths of masts between 100 and 200 ft., and all possible lengths of sighting tube is printed on the tube and gives the corresponding ranges in yards. For the smaller interval, these ranges are of course to be doubled.
measurements: ['one tenth of a foot', 'one twentieth of a foot', '100 and 200 ft.', 'lengths of sighting tube', 'ranges in yards']
interpretation: Measurements of distance by this apparatus can only be very approximate owing to the absence of magnification, uncertainty as regards the length of the mast and its inclination to the line of sight, etc.

description: Two images of the mast are seen in the field of the telescope, one formed by light rays traversing a fixed prism of constant angle, and the other by rays traversing a movable prism of varying angle. These images are made to approach each other until the lower limit of one is level with the upper limit of the other by sliding the movable prism, when the position of an index attached to this permits the range to be read. The movable prism consists of a thin piece of glass, ground concave on both faces, and is attached to a slide worked by a tangent screw. It thus forms a prism of varying angle in front of one half of the telescope, the other half being occupied by the fixed constant angle prism. Ranges up to 3 miles can be read to the nearest tenth of a mile.
interpretation: Assuming that the length of a distant ship’s mast is known, its range can be found by this instrument, which was designed in 1895 for use at sea.

description: This instrument is used to measure ranges in the ordinary manner, by solving a very acute right-angled triangle. The angle subtended at the distant point is constant, whilst the base is variable, and is measured by pacing. Three reflecting right-angled prisms are mounted by hinged joints near the objective of a small telescope, so that any one of the three can be set to reflect rays axially along the telescope from directions at 90°, 88° 51′ 15″ and 74° 53′ 15″ respectively. The first prism is used to set off the base at right angles to the direction of the distant object. The observer paces in the line of the base until, using one of the other two prisms, he again sees the object by reflection. For both observations the telescope is directed to view another distant point at right angles to the target, i.e., in the direction of the base. The number of paces taken between the two observations, multiplied by a constant depending upon the length of pace and the reflecting angle of the second prism used, gives the required range. The constant is determined experimentally.
interpretation: Used to measure ranges by solving a right-angled triangle where the base is measured by pacing.

description: This rangefinder was designed by Capt. Gautier, a French artillery officer, about 1865, and has been extensively used in the French army. Its main feature is a thin prism mounted in a ring at the object end of the sighting tube. By rotating the ring the deviation of rays in the plane of the distant object and the horizontal through the instrument can be varied continuously, and the ring calibrated correspondingly. The sighting tube is about 5 in. long by 1·5 in. diam. and has a protecting tube which can be fitted underneath to serve as a hand-grip when observations are being made. The sighting tube, in addition to the movable ring containing the prism, has a pair of plane mirrors having their faces inclined to each other at an angle of about 45°, and so inclined to the optical axis that rays incident through a window in the side of the tube in a direction nearly perpendicular to the axis, are doubly reflected at the mirrors into the line of the axis, and pass through a small telescope at the eye end of the tube. In the instrument shown, two such telescopes of different powers are fixed side by side. One of the mirrors can be slightly rotated so as to vary the angle of deviation of the reflected rays. In using the instrument, the observer sets the range scale on the movable ring at “infinity” and the index of the movable mirror at the centre. He views the distant object by double reflection at the mirrors and looks directly through the tube and prism for a convenient aiming mark. If such a mark is not quite co-incident with the image of the distant object, he rotates the mirror until coincidence occurs. Then the object and the aiming mark are in directions nearly perpendicular to each other. Next he paces out a convenient distance in the direction of the aiming mark and takes a second observation similar to the first, but this time effects the coincidence by means of the movable prism. He reads off the scale calibrated on that ring when coincidence is effected and multiplies the distance of his base. The result is the range of the distant object. The movable ring is really calibrated to record the reciprocal of the angle of deviation caused by the prism, which is the same as the reciprocal of the angle subtended. by the base at the object. As this base has been made nearly perpendicular to the direction of the object, the product of its length and the reciprocal of the angle gives the range. Thus any convenient base length can be used subject to the condition that it subtends an angle of not more than 3° at the distant object.
interpretation: This rangefinder was designed by Capt. Gautier, a French artillery officer, about 1865, and has been extensively used in the French army. Its main feature is a thin prism mounted in a ring at the object end of the sighting tube. By rotating the ring the deviation of rays in the plane of the distant object and the horizontal through the instrument can be varied continuously, and the ring calibrated correspondingly. description: This type of rangefinder was designed by P. Adie in 1860, and was extensively used by the Admiralty until superseded by the Barr and Stroud pattern. The rangefinder consists of two systems of lenses and right-angled reflecting prisms mounted in a 3-ft. metal tube of square section. Each system forms a “broken” telescope, the objectives being at each end of the tube, along which the rays, originally perpendicular to it, are deflected by right-angled prisms to the centre, where they are again reflected at right angles into the common central eye-piece. In this manner two images of a distant object whose direction is nearly perpendicular to the axis of the tube are obtained, one through each system. These images will be separated laterally by an interval which diminishes continuously as the range increases, but does not become zero until the object is at an infinite distance. If the objective lens and two prisms of one system are separately mounted and can be rotated with respect to the other system, the two images may be made to coincide by such a rotation, and the angle of rotation necessary will vary inversely as the range of the object. This angle can be obtained by calculation, or a table of corresponding values. In the instrument exhibited such an arrangement is effected by mounting one object lens and its pair of reflecting prisms in a separate tube within the main tube containing the other set, and pivoted to this so that the rotation can be effected by a screw threaded in the outer tube with its end pressing against the inner. The angle of rotation is measured by a vernier on one tube and a scale nearest second of arc, and the range read off on a table fixed to the outer leather protecting cover.
interpretation: This type of rangefinder was designed by P. Adie in 1860, and was extensively used by the Admiralty until superseded by the Barr and Stroud pattern. The example shown was used on H.M.S. “Triton” from 1885 to 1904 during the survey of the East Coast of England.
interpretation_source: See British Patent, 1860, No. 357; and 1863, No. 608.

description: A Porro "anallatic" lens is inserted between the objective and eye lenses of this instrument and its horizontal and vertical circles are divided centesimally. It is used in conjunction with a graduated tacheometric staff, upon which the interval subtended between the fixed cross wire varies directly as the distance of the staff from the transverse axis of the instrument, which is itself vertically above the observing station point.
interpretation: The interval subtended between the fixed cross wire on a graduated tacheometric staff varies directly as the distance of the staff from the transverse axis of the instrument. The instrument is used in conjunction with a graduated tacheometric staff.

description: A device to convert a theodolite into a tacheometer for measuring distances, which permits the telescope, when directed upon a graduated staff, to be displaced through a constant small angle, whose limits are determined by two mechanical stops. The distance so measured on the staff will vary directly as the horizontal distance of the staff from the observing station and inversely as the square of the cosine of the altitude angle. As the latter is known, the former can be calculated by using special tables. In the tacheometer invented about 1868 by A. Gentilli, the Austrian engineer, a rigid vertical arm can be clamped to the transverse axis of the telescope in any position. The lower end of this arm can only move a short distance, being limited by two mechanical stops. Consequently the vertical angle through which the telescope can move when clamped to the arm is likewise limited. The instrument in other respects is like an ordinary theodolite of the type made by Stärke about this period. It has a 5-in. horizontal circle and a 3.5-in. vertical quadrant, both reading by vernier and reading microscope to 30'' and having the usual clamps and tangent screws. The telescope has an objective lens of 12 in. focal length and 1.5 in. aperture. The instrument has four levelling screws, two small spirit levels mutually perpendicular on the horizontal circle, and a more sensitive one on the telescope.

interpretation: Used for measuring distances by converting a theodolite into a tacheometer. The instrument is like an ordinary theodolite of the type made by Stärke about this period.

description: An early example of a theodolite modified to enable distances to be measured with it simultaneously with azimuth and altitude angles. This instrument is used in conjunction with a special tacheometric staff having a fixed interval, usually 10 ft., marked upon it. A microscope, rigidly attached with its axis perpendicular to that of the observing telescope, rotating with this telescope about a common transverse axis, measures upon a scale fixed horizontally upon the upper plate of the theodolite the distance traversed when the observing telescope is rotated from the upper mark to the lower mark of the staff. As this staff is always set up vertically, its horizontal distance from the centre of the instrument is inversely proportional to the distance traversed on the scale. The microscope scale is mounted parallel to the telescope at a distance of exactly 6 in. below the transverse axis. It is 4 in. long and is graduated to read 0·02 in. directly, whilst it can be moved on the plate, parallel to its own length, through a small interval by means of a micrometer screw with a graduated drum, which measures 0·002 of each division of the scale. In this manner the ultimate graduation of the scale corresponds to 4 × 10⁻⁵ in. so that, if n such divisions are traversed when the theodolite rotates from the upper to the lower mark of the staff, the distance of this staff from the instrument will be 15 × 10³ ÷ n ft. In other respects the instrument is similar to an ordinary transit repeating theodolite. Slow-motion tangent screws are provided for each circle, and the usual spirit-levels on the plate and telescope. A diagonal eyepiece is fitted to the microscope for convenience in taking steep sights.

description: A 4-metre wooden staff, graduated in centimetres and used in conjunction with the tacheometer. It is inextensible, and does not materially differ from a levelling rod. The graduation marks are black bands, 1 cm. wide, at intervals of 1 cm. Those corresponding to metres and decimetres extend right across the face, the rest only half across. The metres are numbered by large red numbers and the decimetres by smaller black numbers. The half-decimetre points are marked by small black arrows. The rod has a rectangular section, 3 in. wide by 1 1/4 in. deep, and the face is slightly sunk below the edges to prevent abrasion of the graduations.
interpretation: Used in conjunction with the tacheometer. Does not materially differ from a levelling rod.

description: A photograph of two ancient Egyptian levels. Each level consists of a wooden frame in the shape of an isosceles triangle, having its sides equally prolonged beyond the base. The ends of the legs are cut parallel to the cross piece, so that the frame may rest upon a flat surface. A plummet is suspended from the apex of the frame, and its cord passes over the front of the cross piece, in the middle of which is engraved a vertical mark. If the cord lies along this mark when the plummet hangs freely, the surface on which the level rests is horizontal. Hieroglyphics are engraved in the face of the lower level.
interpretation: The original levels are of the A-shaped plummet type, exhibited in the Cairo Museum and are of considerable antiquity. Such levels were used by builders and engineers of all the early civilizations and have survived in use to the present date without fundamental modification.

description: A metal triangle which can be freely suspended by means of two brass pins so that its two equal sides are vertical and horizontal respectively. All objects in the prolongation of its third side will then be at a horizontal distance from the instrument equal to their height above it. The former distance can be measured, and the height thus ascertained. The hypotenuse of the metal triangle has a pair of sights which enable objects in its line to be viewed. When using the instrument, the observer takes up a position from which he can sight the object whose height is required, the instrument being freely suspended. He then measures his horizontal distance from a point vertically beneath the object. This distance is equal to the height of the object above the eye-level of the observer. When not in use, the instrument fits in the wooden case exhibited with it.
interpretation: Used for measuring the height of objects by determining their horizontal distance from the observer.

description: This is a level of a type much used for rough levelling during the 17th century, and probably dates from the latter half of that period. It consists of a heavy tube freely suspended from the top of a wooden case by a thread attached to its centre. The tube has a horizontal slit at one end, and a corresponding cross wire at the other; glass windows in the ends of the wooden case permit a free view along the sights. The instrument as a whole can be rotated in azimuth upon its stand. When not in use, the sighting tube can be fixed by means of two screws passing through the bottom of the wooden case. In this instrument, the centre of gravity of the suspended tube is very little, if any, below the line of sight. Hence the tube is very sensitive to disturbances, which is a source of trouble. Moreover, there is no easy method of adjusting the line of sight to be truly horizontal. Owing to these defects, both of which were remedied in the more precise instruments on the "balance" principle designed by Huygens, this type of level is not very accurate. The body of the tube is made of lead, the ends containing the sights being of brass. The wooden case is screwed into the top of a small column, provided with a brass socket at its other end. The socket serves to attach the level to its stand, which may be a tripod or simply a "stick" stand.
interpretation: Used for rough levelling during the 17th century. The instrument is sensitive to disturbances and lacks an easy method for adjusting the line of sight to be horizontal, making it not very accurate compared to later designs.

description: This instrument consists of a brass alidade attached to a semi-circle, pivoted upon a heavy stand, which is set with its base horizontal by means of a small brass plummet. The semi-circle and alidade can be rotated in the vertical plane, and the inclination of the line of sight read by a fixed index on the stand. The semi-circle is graduated in degrees and has a diameter of 4·2 in. The sight rule is a hollow tube fitted with dual sights at each end, one set being within the tube and the other on top of it in the opposite sense.
interpretation: Used for measuring inclination.

description: This is a German instrument made in 1755, and consists of a hollow wooden stand with a flat base and brass facings. A brass plummet is suspended down one face, and by its position on a scale of degrees engraved on the lower part of the face measures the inclination of the base of the instrument. No sights are provided. A brass knob, screwed into the top of the stand can be detached and used as a plummet; a cord wound round a drum inside the stand is used to suspend the knob. The plummet has a length of 4·8 in., which is the radius of the graduated arc. This extends 15° on either side of the vertical.
interpretation: Measures the inclination of the base of the instrument.

description: This instrument can be used for testing whether a surface is horizontal, vertical or inclined at 45°. It consists of a loaded disc, pivoted between the vertical faces of a cylindrical brass case fixed to a brass ruler. Marks engraved on the edge of the revolving disc show by their coincidence with marks on the fixed case whether the ruler, which is placed on the surface to be tested, is horizontal, vertical, or inclined at 45°. The ruler has a length of about 6 in., and one of its bevelled edges is graduated in millimetres.
interpretation: Used for testing whether a surface is horizontal, vertical or inclined at 45°.

description: This type of level was invented by Col. Burel in 1829, and operates upon the principle that in a vertically suspended mirror the eye sees a reflected image of itself at its own level. The instrument consists of a rectangular frame, suspended in gimbal bearings so as to hang vertical owing to its own weight. The frame contains a piece of plane glass, of which one vertical half is silvered and the other half left free for direct vision of a distant object. A horizontal cross wire bisects the two parts. The observer holds the instrument in front of his eye and moves it until he sees the reflected image of his eye bisected by the cross wire. Any distant object then intersected by the wire will be at the level of his eye.
interpretation: Operates upon the principle that in a vertically suspended mirror the eye sees a reflected image of itself at its own level. The observer holds the instrument in front of his eye and moves it until he sees the reflected image of his eye bisected by the cross wire. Any distant object then intersected by the wire will be at the level of his eye.

description: This is very similar to the adjacent Burel type, but has a heavy screw threaded in the base of the frame. By working the screw the inclination of the plane of the mirror can be varied, and adjusted to be truly vertical by means of a test sight. The mirror also occupies much more than half of the frame, leaving a small part only for direct vision.
interpretation: Used for adjusting the inclination of a mirror to be truly vertical by means of a test sight.

description: A heavy arc is attached to the lower part of the mirror frame and can be turned into the same plane as the mirror for convenience of carriage, or into a perpendicular frame for measuring angles of elevation or depression. In the latter position the weight of the arc causes the mirror plane to take up an inclination to the vertical, which can be varied by means of a movable radial arm, concentric with the arc and carrying a sliding counterpoise at its extremity. The arc is so graduated on its edge that the position of one edge of the movable arm gives the inclination of the mirror, and, therefore, of the line of sight between the observer's eye and its reflection in the mirror. The arc is graduated to read gradients from zero to 1 in 5.

description: This level was constructed in the early part of the 19th century and used in 1831 by J. A. Lloyd, F.R.S., in ascertaining the differences of level between the Thames at London Bridge, Sheerness and various intermediate points. The telescope has a focal length of 28 in. and is finally levelled by means of a 12-in. spirit level mounted at one side parallel to its axis. The objective lens of the telescope has a 2-in. aperture, and is fixed in the tube, the eyepiece tube being focussed by a rack and pinion arrangement and having a fixed diaphragm and a slide focussing Ramsden inverting eyepiece. The telescope is attached to a transverse horizontal axis, which rests in Y-s on standards fixed to the horizontal plate. The telescope is supported near both ends by vertical screws threaded in the ends of a rigid bar fixed to the horizontal plate parallel to the axis of the telescope. These screws are used in the final adjustment of the telescope axis, which is tested by the main spirit level. This bar is suspended from the ends of a metal rod fixed on one side of the telescope, and has ivory scales graduated to thirtieths of an inch mounted above its bubble-tube. A small level is also fixed transversely at one end of the main level. The bubble of the latter moves over one division of the scale when the telescope is elevated about 2 seconds of arc. The horizontal plate can rotate about a vertical axis, and has a clamp and tangent screw for slow motion. It is attached to a pair of parallel plates, connected by four levelling screws of the usual type. A small circular spirit-level is fixed to the plate above its centre for setting it horizontal. The telescope can be reversed in its Y-s end for end, or rotated through 180° about its own axis, as in all Y-levels.

description: A spirit level with a 30-in. telescope mounted in Y-s in a manner similar to the ordinary Y-level, but is fitted with an extra spirit level suspended above the telescope, and also has a circular supporting base resembling that of a large theodolite and resting on three footscrews. The objective lens of the telescope has a 2-in. aperture and is fixed in the tube, the eyepiece tube having a rack and pinion focussing movement. The eyepiece is of the Ramsden inverting type and is also focussed by a rack and pinion movement. Gun-metal collars are shrunk on to the telescope near its extremities and rest in Y-s fixed to the horizontal circle. One of these Y-s can be adjusted vertically by means of a screw. This adjustment serves to level the telescope more precisely than is possible with the footscrews. The 14-in. horizontal circle can rotate about a vertical axis, and has a clamp and tangent screw. It also carries a central 31-in. compass, graduated in degrees, and a small thermometer. The supporting base of the instrument consists of two horizontal circles of 14 in. diameter connected by three vertical pillars to which the three foot-screws are fixed. Beneath the telescope a 17-in. spirit level is mounted in adjustable bearings, and a 22-in. level of similar construction can be suspended above the telescope from pivots carried by brackets fixed to the end of the tube. Both pivots are adjustable. Each level has ivory scales, graduated to twentieths of an inch mounted above its tube. Small transverse levels are also fixed to the telescope and at one end of the suspended level.

description: Troughton type spirit level. A small compass, supported on four pillars, is provided for traversing. The telescope has an aperture of 1 1/4 in. and a focal length of 15 in., and is provided with stops. The eyepiece tube is focussed by a rack and pinion arrangement actuated by a screw. The diaphragm can easily be disclosed for examination by removing the eyepiece. There are two eyepieces provided, one erect and the other inverting. The bubble-tube is 10 in. long, and has a radius of curvature of about 50 ft., giving a motion of the bubble of 1/5 in. for every minute of arc. The compass ring is 2 1/2 in. in diameter, and is graduated to read single degrees.

interpretation: This level was formerly the property of George Stephenson, and was used by him at Chat Moss in the survey for the Manchester and Liverpool Railway. It is of the type designed and constructed by Troughton, the spirit-level being rigidly fixed in the telescope, which is not reversible, as in the Ramsden type. Such an instrument, whilst incapable of preliminary adjustment, is very simple and rigid in construction, and is well suited for engineering surveys.

description: This instrument was made about the middle of the 19th century, and was used until 1907 for levelling minor lines. The spirit level is attached by adjusting screws to the telescope, which fits in Y-shaped bearings, and can be rotated or reversed in these for adjustment of the line of collimation. The parallel plate arrangement for levelling the instrument is of the usual type, with four levelling-screws, axis clamp and tangent-screw for slow-motion. The diaphragm containing a horizontal and vertical wire is easily accessible after unscrewing the eyepiece, which is arranged to give an erect image of the staff.

description: This level was made between 1840 and 1850 and was used for levelling of second-order lines. The spirit level is graduated to read 5 seconds of elevation, and is attached to the telescope, which rests in Y-shaped bearings, and can be rotated or reversed for adjustment of the line of collimation. A compass is provided for rough traversing, and an elevating screw permits the telescope to be finally levelled with great accuracy. In the diaphragm are two vertical and one horizontal wires. The eyepiece is adjusted for parallax by a sliding tube arrangement, whilst the telescope is focussed on the staff by a rack and pinion which moves the objective. The compass-ring has a diameter of 3 1/4 in. and is graduated to read single degrees. The spirit level tube is 10 in. long, and is graduated at intervals of 1/4 in., each interval corresponding to 5 seconds of arc. The parallel plate arrangement is of the usual type, and a slow-motion tangent screw is provided for azimuth setting.

description: This level has a telescope of 2·2-in. aperture and 23-in. focal length, with a 12-in. spirit level attached, reading to single seconds of arc. The telescope rests in Y bearings, in which it can be rotated and also reversed end for end, for adjustments. A small transverse level is also provided on the telescope for rough levelling, whilst the final accurate setting is performed by means of an elevating screw, which moves one bearing. The instrument has a 5⅛-in. compass fitted to its alidade for rough traversing, the compass being graduated in single degrees. There is also the usual parallel-plate levelling arrangement, with four screws, for setting the alidade approxi- mately horizontal. A slow motion tangent screw is provided for setting the instru- ment accurately in azimuth. The telescope has a micrometer eyepiece, and is focussed on the staff by moving the eyepiece tube. The spirit level has an ivory scale above each end, graduated in 1/20 in., each division corresponding to about 2 seconds of arc of elevation.

description: A level of this type, serving also for measuring inclines and distances by means of the elevating screw, is particularly adapted by reason of its compactness and simplicity of construction for preliminary surveys where no great accuracy is required. It consists of a small telescope and spirit-level separately mounted upon a platform connected with a tripod by means of a ball-and-socket joint of a special type, often employed in small surveying instruments of German construction. This joint permits the orientation of the platform to be varied, whilst leaving it perfectly free to rotate in azimuth about the socket, which is fixed to the tripod. The platform terminates underneath in a metal ball, at the lower end of which is a cylindrical pin. The socket consists of two parts screwed together, an upper spherical dome enclosing the ball, and a lower tubular sheath surrounding the pin. Two levelling screws, set perpendicularly to each other, work in threads in this sheath, and impinge upon a metal collar which encircles the pin sufficiently tightly to prevent shake, but not to hinder the free azimuthal rotation of the pin, and consequently the platform. Opposite the two screws, and likewise impinging on the collar is a spring which takes the pressure of the screws. By means of these screws the platform can be set level in all directions. The spirit level can be adjusted upon the platform by the small screws at one end of its case, whilst the telescope can be elevated or depressed about an axis at one end fixed in the platform by means of a fine-threaded screw at the other end.

Particularly adapted by reason of its compactness and simplicity of construction for preliminary surveys where no great accuracy is required. By this means, as in tacheometry, distances can be measured with fair accuracy.

description: This instrument, primarily designed for levelling, can also be employed for measuring angles in any plane, and is likewise provided with stadia lines in diaphragm of the telescope for measuring distances. It is thus a type of cheap, portable, universal instrument, specially adapted for surveys of minor precision. The special features which distinguish it from an ordinary small level are the graduated semicircle and the peculiar method of attaching the spirit level to the telescope and the whole instrument to the tripod. The lower parallel plate is not attached directly to the tripod head, but to an intermediate knuckle-joint piece, which permits the instrument as a whole to be set with the semicircle in any plane. The spirit level can also be attached to the telescope in two places, one serving when the semicircle is horizontal and the other when it is vertical. The telescope can rotate on the semicircle, which is graduated to 30 minutes and reads by vernier to 2 minutes, and the semicircle can likewise rotate irrespective of the telescope, thus permitting angles to be “repeated.” The parallel plate arrangement is of the usual type, with four levelling screws.

It is thus a type of cheap, portable, universal instrument, specially adapted for surveys of minor precision.

description: A later modification of a level designed and constructed by F. W. Breithaupt in 1845, with the idea of minimizing the instrumental adjustments usually necessary as a preliminary to taking levels. The method of weighting the main spirit level and suspending it freely in pin bearings attached to the telescope enables the surveyor to compensate by double readings the errors arising from non-parallelism of the spirit-level axis, telescope axis, and line of sight. In this level the telescope can be rotated in its collars through a complete half-turn, the extreme positions being determined by mechanical stops. The spirit level, whilst revolving with the telescope, does not rotate, but is kept with its engraved scale uppermost. Consequently the bubble is always visible against the scale, and its variation during the rotation measures the extent to which the axis of the spirit level is inclined to the axis of rotation of the telescope. Such an inclination, if small, will be automatically rendered ineffective provided two readings of the levelling staff are made with the spirit level “centred,” one before the telescope is rotated in its collars through 180°, and the other after. This double reading also corrects for lack of coincidence between the mechanical axis of rotation of the telescope and the line of sight. The mean of the two readings will be the true reading which would be obtained if the three axes of spirit level, telescope rings and vision were mutually parallel. Thus it is not necessary to adjust the instrument beforehand for this parallelism. It is, however, essential that the spirit level itself should be so adjusted that when its bubble is central, its own axis of rotation reversing the spirit level in its bearings should be horizontal. This can be tested by centring the bubble, and reading the bubble again. Half the difference is removed by the means of the two capstan-headed screws which fix one end of the bubble tube to its case. To enable the spirit level to be so reversed, one bearing pin can be withdrawn from its supporting bracket. The lower part of the instrument is provided with a circular box level, which serves to set the main axis nearly vertical by means of the footscrews. No attempt is made to render this axis exactly vertical, as the telescope is always finally levelled by means of the elevating screw. The head of this latter is divided, and serves to measure very accurately small gradients. The diaphragm of the telescope has two horizontal subtense wires in addition to the central levelling wires, so that the instrument can be used to measure distances.

interpretation: This is a later modification of a level designed and constructed by F. W. Breithaupt in 1845, with the idea of minimizing the instrumental adjustments usually necessary as a preliminary to taking levels. The method of weighting the main spirit level and suspending it freely in pin bearings attached to the telescope enables the surveyor to compensate by double readings the errors arising from non-parallelism of the spirit-level axis, telescope axis, and line of sight. In this level the telescope can be rotated in its collars through a complete half-turn, the extreme positions being determined by mechanical stops. The spirit level, whilst revolving with the telescope, does not rotate, but is kept with its engraved scale uppermost. Consequently the bubble is always visible against the scale, and its variation during the rotation measures the extent to which the axis of the spirit level is inclined to the axis of rotation of the telescope. Such an inclination, if small, will be automatically rendered ineffective provided two readings of the levelling staff are made with the spirit level “centred,” one before the telescope is rotated in its collars through 180°, and the other after. This double reading also corrects for lack of coincidence between the mechanical axis of rotation of the telescope and the line of sight. The mean of the two readings will be the true reading which would be obtained if the three axes of spirit level, telescope rings and vision were mutually parallel. Thus it is not necessary to adjust the instrument beforehand for this parallelism. It is, however, essential that the spirit level itself should be so adjusted that when its bubble is central, its own axis of rotation reversing the spirit level in its bearings should be horizontal. This can be tested by centring the bubble, and reading the bubble again. Half the difference is removed by the means of the two capstan-headed screws which fix one end of the bubble tube to its case. To enable the spirit level to be so reversed, one bearing pin can be withdrawn from its supporting bracket. The lower part of the instrument is provided with a circular box level, which serves to set the main axis nearly vertical by means of the footscrews. No attempt is made to render this axis exactly vertical, as the telescope is always finally levelled by means of the elevating screw. The head of this latter is divided, and serves to measure very accurately small gradients. The diaphragm of the telescope has two horizontal subtense wires in addition to the central levelling wires, so that the instrument can be used to measure distances. The “suspension” spirit level of the type here shown was soon superseded in compensating levels by Amsler’s two-sided “reversion” level, which is much less liable to be injured by shocks than Breithaupt’s pattern.

description: This clinometer is not provided with sights, but has two plane edges at right angles and a movable spirit-level with a vernier at one end. The instrument is set on the face of the rod and the level rotated until the bubble is centred, when the zero mark of the vernier gives the inclination to a sixteenth of a degree. The arc over which the vernier moves is graduated in half degrees, each of the eight intervals between the vernier graduations being seven-eighths of a half degree. The spirit level is very sensitive, and the bubble moves about 0·5 cm. for every variation of a sixteenth of a degree in the inclination.
interpretation: An instrument of this type is principally used for setting levelling-rods vertical, or for measuring the gradient of a rod used for determining distances in cadastral surveys. It can be set upon some kind of sighting rod and used for measuring gradients or for levelling.

description: This instrument was made in the first half of the 19th century, and is used for measuring the elevation to the horizontal of any inclined plane on which it can be set. It is not provided with sights. It consists of two brass rulers, hinged at one end. The upper ruler carries a sensitive 6-in. spirit level and an index, which moves over a graduated brass arc fixed to the lower ruler. This latter is placed upon the surface to be measured and the other ruler revolved until the bubble of the level is centred, when it can be clamped by a screw on the index plate and the reading taken. The arc is graduated in degrees from 0° to 50°.
interpretation: Used for measuring the elevation to the horizontal of any inclined plane on which it can be set. The arc is graduated in degrees from 0° to 50°.

description: An instrument with two brass rulers hinged together at one end. A 3-in. spirit level is supported parallel to the upper ruler in bearings on the sights. The lower ruler has a socket for fixing the instrument to a stand.

description: In a hand-level it is desirable that the object sighted and the levelling mechanism should be simultaneously visible. The combined level and clinometer designed by Capt. Abney, R.E., about the year 1870, utilizes the idea of reflecting the bubble of a spirit level into the line of sight of the sighting tube by means of a diagonal mirror fixed in one half of the latter, the other half being left free for sighting the object. This device had been previously used on a sextant. In the instrument exhibited, a graduated semicircle is rigidly fixed to the rectangular sighting tube, which has a pin-hole aperture and a diagonal mirror fixed beneath a slit in its upper face, vertically beneath the centre of the arc. Through this centre passes an axis, carrying a small transversely mounted spirit level at one extremity and a vernier arm near the other, which terminates in a large milled wheel. On rotating this wheel the spirit level is set at any angle to the line of sight, the angle being measured by the position of the vernier on the graduated arc. The cover of the spirit level has apertures above and below, the latter permitting an image of the bubble to be seen after reflection on the mirror, whilst the former is used when the clinometer is set on the surface whose gradient is required. The arc is graduated in degrees up to 60° on both sides of the vertical, and reads by vernier on the movable arm to 10 minutes. It also has a scale of gradients to 1 in 1, read by the edge of the vernier.

description: This example differs from the preceding one in minor details. A modern Service clinometer for measuring to the nearest minute the angle of elevation of a plane surface. The angle is measured to the nearest degree by a rotating arm which traverses a fixed graduated sector attached to the base. The arm is slightly curved on its upper and lower surfaces, and carries a sliding spirit level whose position, when the bubble is central with respect to the scale graduated on the arm, gives the number of minutes in the angle. There are two flat mutually perpendicular base plates, one painted black and the other red, and the sector of degrees is graduated on both sides, one set numbered in black from o to 44 and the other in red from 50 to 89, for use with the corresponding base. description: Instead of a graduated arc, this type of clinometer is provided with a rotatable drum, upon the face of which is a graduated spiral groove, upon which is recorded the amount of elevation of the surface tested. The bubble level is mounted within a gunmetal frame which has two surfaces accurately machined at right angles to each other. One end of the level is pivoted to the frame, and the other end is kept pressed against the base of the drum which rotates upon a threaded screw carried by the frame. As the drum rotates, an index on the scale the resulting elevation of the free end of the level above the pivoted end, and hence, when the bubble is centred, the elevation of the plane upon which the frame is set. No sights are provided with this instrument, which is designed for recording the slope of a plane surface with respect to the vertical or horizontal, according to which of the two plane surfaces of the instrument is in contact with the surface tested. The range of the drum scale is from 40 minutes below to 45° above zero, the first 5° being subdivided by dots to 1 minute; thereafter lines indicate every 5 minutes.

description: In this clinometer, one sight is fixed and the other is movable over a graduated scale engraved upon the vane; the position of the movable sight registers the inclination of the line of sight. The instrument consists of a hollow bubble arm mounted upon a gunmetal base, which has three studs on its lower face. The bubble arm is pivoted at one end to the base, and carries an adjusting screw at its other end for setting the bubble central. A folding sight vane is fitted to each end of the bubble arm, the shorter vane having a fixed aperture backsight and the longer one carrying the sliding foresight. The latter vane has two scales engraved upon it, one of degrees, subdivided to 20 minutes, and the other of tangents. The range of the scale is 0°-23° of elevation or depression.

description: A spirit level for testing the horizontality of a telescope axis, suspended from the axis by curved brackets. It features a bubble tube about 15 in. long by 1 1/4 in. diameter, with an ivory scale mounted on the casing and divided in tenth-inches. The brass casing of the bubble tube has end plates that fit loosely upon screwed vertical pins and can be clamped in any desired position by upper and lower capstan nuts. The pins project from a horizontal brass tube, somewhat longer than the bubble tube and having suspension brackets fastened to its ends. The upper portions of these brackets are curved and their ends turned over and provided with inverted V-plates which rest on the telescope axis. The scale divisions are numbered symmetrically from the centre. A small transverse spirit level is mounted on one end of the casing of the main level. The vertical pin at one end of the base tube is slightly adjustable by means of capstan nuts.
interpretation: In large astronomical and surveying instruments, specially long and sensitive levels are generally provided for testing the horizontality of the telescope axis. The levels are usually fitted above the axis by bearing forks, but are sometimes suspended from it by curved brackets.

description: This exhibit comprises twenty-two bubble tubes of various shapes, sizes and sensitivities, all except two being unmounted. Six are of the circular or “pill-box” type, the upper surface of the container being internally ground spherical, so that the bubble, when centred, occupies the space inside a circle engraved on the glass. Two of this type, which are not very sensitive and are only used for rough levelling, are shown mounted in brass cases, attached to the base-board. The remaining sixteen are tube levels, six of them having their glass containers bent as a whole into a circular shape, and the other ten being straight tubes, internally ground to various curvatures according to the desired sensitivity. The first six are not very sensitive, and are of the type used by carpenters, masons, etc. The other ten are used on surveying instruments, etc., and are usually mounted in brass cases, attached to the instrument by adjustable screws. On the larger levels of this type, division marks are graduated at 0·1 in. interval for reading the positions of the ends of the bubble, and the sensitivity is indicated by the angle of elevation of the level necessary to cause the bubble to move over one division. The most sensitive one exhibited has a sensitivity of 1 division per 5·5 seconds of elevation. This particular bubble tube has also a separate chamber at one end. When the bubble expands owing to increasing temperature, a portion of the air can be detached and transferred to the supplementary chamber through a small aperture in the separating wall, and the bubble thus reduced to its normal size.

description: A graduated wooden rod 6 ft. long, 1 in. wide, and in. deep, over which can slide a sighting vane, which has a sharply defined diamond of dark wood inlaid upon a face of light wood, and fits closely to the face of the rod. The vane is moved by the observer signals that it is in line with the telescope, when the former takes the reading of an index mark on the bevelled edge of a small opening in the vane. The face of the staff is graduated both in inches, divided to tenths, and also in hundredths of a foot along its whole length save the top 3 in. Another rod of slightly smaller section can slide along the back of the first, being retained in position by a metal band which serves as a friction clamp. This second rod is not divided and merely serves as a stand for extending the graduated rod. Both are tipped with brass at their ends. A second vane, similar to the first, is supplied. Each has a circular shape, of diameter 5 in. The inlaid diamond has diagonals 5 in. and 2 in., the longer bisecting the vane horizontally. Pins and a metal spring fixed to the back of the vane keep it in position on the rod.

description: This is an inextensible wooden staff 10·5 ft. long, having a rectangular section 2 in. wide by 1 in. deep, and is graduated in hundredths of a foot so as to be read through the telescope by the observer himself. The face of the staff is sunk slightly below the edges to preserve the graduations from abrasion. The graduation marks consist of black horizontal bands 0·01 ft. wide at uniform intervals of 0·01 ft. apart. The 0·1-ft. bands stretch right across the staff, the remainder occupying the left portion only, save at the 0·05-ft. points, where there is an additional black mark to the right of the corresponding white band. Large black numbers, horizontally set, mark the feet, the tenths being marked by smaller black numbers set vertically. A diamond is used instead of the number “five” on the latter graduations, and a dot is placed near the “nine” to distinguish it from the “six” when the numbers are seen inverted in the field of the telescope.

description: This exhibit illustrates the method of engraving wooden and invar rules for their levelling rods now adopted by Messrs. Watts. The portions to be painted black on the white surface of the rule are first gouged out to a sufficient depth and the black filled in nearly flush with the white surface; the black bands are thus rendered very durable. Two of the rules are portions of those used in the ordinary Sopwith type of staff, one showing the graduations cut and the strips gouged out, the other the finished rule, with the strips filled in and figured. The third rule is made of invar, for use in a precise levelling rod, and the bands of black at 0.02-ft. intervals are not so wide as in the other type of rod, where they are exactly 0.01 ft. wide. In the latter case the lower edges of the bands define the odd hundredths of a foot and the upper edges the even hundredths; in the invar rod, only the upper edges are used, the cross wire of the telescope being made to coincide with this edge in taking a reading. The graduations are not figured on the invar strip, but on the surrounding wood of the rod, as in the adjacent exhibit of a portion of the complete rod.
