object_name: PORTION OF INVAR PRECISE LEVELLING ROD
description: The lower portion of a levelling rod used in precise surveys. The invar rule is painted white and engraved with black bands at intervals of 0.02 ft., every fifth band extending over the complete width (about 2 cm.) of the rule, and the others over half its width. The rule is then screwed into a central recess in the face of the wooden rod, which has an I section for strength and lightness, and is shod with a metal shoe terminating in a flat base plate; the bottom of the invar rule is flush with this plate. The face of the wooden rod is painted white and numbered opposite the marks corresponding to intervals of 0.1 ft. on the invar rule. The numbers are in black, and are inverted so as to be seen erect in the telescope of the level; a V is used instead of 5 and an N instead of 9. At the divisions of the rule corresponding to an integral number of feet from the base plate, large red numbers are painted on the wood, and are twice repeated in smaller sized numbers on the opposite side of the face so that the observer has always one of the red numbers in the telescope field.

interpretation: The advantages of a metal scale for levelling staves have until recently been counterbalanced by the tendency of such scales to expand when heated, and the difficulty of ascertaining their temperature in order to apply the necessary correction. The invention of “invar”—a nickel-steel alloy of negligible temperature coefficient—has now led to its employment in levelling rods used in precise surveys. In estimating the position of the cross wire with respect to the graduated scale of the rod, the nearest 0.02-ft. mark is taken and the remaining interval found either by elevating or depressing the telescope by a fine-motion screw, or by moving an optical device which causes the image of the rod to be raised or lowered in the telescope field. The position of the cross wire is thus readily found to 0.001 ft.

description: This instrument is a closed cistern mercury barometer of the type common in the late 18th and early 19th centuries; it is specially adapted for portability and thus capable of employment in measuring altitudes. When it is being transported, the mercury can be forced up so as to fill the tube completely by turning an adjusting screw, which depresses the flexible leather base of the cistern. The aperture in the wooden case, used for reading the height of the mercury and the temperature, can also be closed by a rotating brass sheath. The barometer is graduated in inches, and reads by a vernier index, operated by a rack and pinion mechanism, to 0.002 in. A thermometer, provided with Centigrade and Fahrenheit scales, is placed near the top of the instrument. A suspension ring is fixed at the top, and is covered by a ferrule when the instrument is being carried. A screw cap at the bottom likewise serves to enclose the adjusting screw which operates on the cistern. The wooden case which encloses the lower part of the tube is graduated in inches, so that the instrument can serve as a rough measuring rod.
interpretation: Specially adapted for portability and thus capable of employment in measuring altitudes. The wooden case which encloses the lower part of the tube is graduated in inches, so that the instrument can serve as a rough measuring rod.

interpretation: This resembles the adjacent instrument, made by West, in its general character- istics of compactness and portability, but differs in the arrangement of the cistern. This is of the usual flexible base type, but has a supplementary syphon tube, connected to the cistern by a narrow neck, which can be closed by means of a cock. When the instrument is being used, the cock is opened, and the mercury allowed to attain a fixed height in the syphon tube. This is the zero of the barometer tube scale. For transporting the barometer, the mercury is withdrawn from the syphon tube and the cock closed, after which the flexible base of the cistern is de- pressed by means of the adjusting screw until the mercury completely fills the barometer tube. The barometer tube is graduated in inches, and read to 0·002 in. by a vernier attached to the movable index. A thermometer with Centigrade and Fahrenheit scales is fixed near the top. The window for reading this and the barometer can be closed by means of a rotating brass shutter, and a similar shutter at the bottom of the instrument serves to protect the cistern and syphon tube when required.

description: The Gay-Lussac syphon-tube mercury barometer, in which both the long and short tubes are closed completely at the end, but a small aperture in the side of the short tube permits the air to enter whilst preventing the mercury escaping, was essentially a portable instrument, and was, therefore, often used for measuring altitudes prior to the invention of the aneroid. The instrument exhibited is of this type. The barometer tube is enclosed in a brass case, at the ends of which are cork cushions. Scales graduated directly to 0·02 in. and read by movable verniers to 0·001 in. are engraved upon the case opposite the ends of the mercury. Each vernier has an index which can be set level with the top of the mercury column. The difference between the two readings then gives the height of the barometer. A thermometer, with Centigrade and Fahrenheit graduations, is fixed near the centre of the tube. This instrument is attached by brackets to a wooden stand, and can be set accurately vertical by means of three screws threaded in the lower bracket with their ends pressing against the case of the barometer. For mountain barometers a tripod stand was usually provided.
interpretation: A portable instrument often used for measuring altitudes prior to the invention of the aneroid. Scales are engraved to read differences in height of the barometer.

interpretation: This instrument was made about 1890, for the use of surveyors in measuring altitudes up to 4,000 ft. The zero mark of the altitude scale corresponds to a height of 32 in. in the mercury barometer. The altitude scale has a diam. of 3·5 in., and is graduated every 10 ft., single feet being estimated. The movable glass cover carries an index mark, which is set to the last height read, and a small lens for facilitating reading. The altitude scale is slightly raised on a step so that its inside graduated edge is flush with an aluminium plate fixed to the tip of the hand and provided with a mark. By this arrangement errors due to parallax are avoided. The instrument is compensated for temperature variations.

description: In aneroid barometers many attempts have been made to provide scales suitable for a very extended range of altitudes. This instrument shows the three concentric circular scale arrangement devised by Major H. S. S. Watkin, by which altitudes from zero to 10,860 ft. can be measured. The zero graduation corresponds to a height of 31 in. in the mercury barometer. Altitudes from zero to 3,440 ft. are marked at 20 ft. intervals on the outermost scale, which has a diameter of 3·6 in. The middle scale, of diam. 2·9 in., records altitudes from 3,440 ft. to 6,860 ft., whilst the innermost scale, of diam. 2·2 in., completes the range to 10,860 ft., every 20 ft. being marked on each scale. The corresponding mercury barometer scales are marked at 0·02 in. intervals from 31 in. to 20 in. To show which scale should be used, an indicator exhibits the number 1, 2 or 3, corresponding to the outer, middle and inner scales respectively. The number indicated is marked upon a plate worked by the mechanism, and is automatically altered when the barometer hand reaches the end of the scale concerned. The breaks in the circles are indicated by black bars. The revolving glass cover carries an index hand, which can be set to the last reading taken. The instrument is compensated for temperature variations.

description: A new “thermometrical barometer” of the type here exhibited was invented by Wollaston and described by him before the Royal Society in 1817. The one exhibited was made before 1821. It is essentially a very sensitive “boiling-point” thermometer, whereby the temperature at which water boils may be found to within a thousandth of a degree Fahrenheit, and the altitude of the place determined accordingly. The bulb of the thermometer is spherical and has a diameter of about an inch. The tube has a length of 30 in. and a very fine bore, so that one degree Fahrenheit corresponds to a movement of the mercury in the tube of 4 in. This is measured by means of a brass scale fixed on the face of the rod which supports the tube. The scale is graduated to read 0·02° F. directly, and 0·002° F. by means of a movable vernier. The rod carries a double walled tin cylinder surrounding the bulb of the thermometer. The cylinder can be detached and partly filled with water, which is then boiled by means of a spirit lamp so that the steam surrounds the bulb of the thermometer. Along the side of the rod is attached a strip of paper on which is marked a scale of corrections to be applied to the temperature scale, owing probably to inequalities in the diameter of the bore of the tube.

description: A hypsometer for determining altitudes by means of the boiling point of water. The example shown is of the “pocket” type much used by Alpine travellers. Its thermometer is graduated from 180° to 215° F. by 0·02°. The apparatus consists of a brass water container and steam jacket, in which the thermometer is suspended and which is fixed above a small spirit lamp for boiling the water. A brass case surrounds the lamp, which is further screened from wind by means of a black japanned tin box, provided with air holes covered by wire gauze. The thermometer is suspended with its bulb inside an inner tube connected to the boiler. An outer telescopic tube surrounds this and serves to support the thermometer in addition to forming a steam jacket enclosing the mercury as much as possible. The steam escapes by a hole in the top of this outer tube. In improved hypsometers it is made to retrace its path downwards and escape at the bottom of the steam jacket.
interpretation: Although not so accurate as a standard barometer, a hypsometer for determining altitudes by means of the boiling point of water is more convenient for rapid surveys in mountainous districts. With this apparatus altitudes are determined by means of specially prepared tables provided with the instrument, giving the heights above sea level corresponding to a particular temperature at which water boils, and also corrections to be made for latitude, mean temperature of the air, and decrease of gravity with increase of elevation.

description: A reproduction of a Roman groma. The original instrument consisted of a cross, composed of two equal perpendicular arms intersecting at their centres, mounted upon a supporting staff (ferramentum), upon which the cross could revolve in azimuth: from the ends of the cross were suspended four plummets, through which sights were taken by the surveyor. This reconstruction comprises all the foregoing portions, with the additional modification that the cross is not supported directly upon the staff, but is pivoted upon the outer end of a curved bracket, which is in turn mounted rotatably upon the head of the staff. This arrangement enables the centre of the cross to be set above the mark on a boundary stone, whilst the staff is driven into the ground beside the stone; also, sights could be taken through opposite, not adjacent, plumb lines without interference from the staff. The wooden staff, which is nearly 2 metres long, terminates at its lower end in a fluted iron shoe, and is encircled at its upper extremity by a brass collar, along its upper and lower faces by curved brass strips, and terminating at the staff end in a brass collar and at the cross end in a brass pivot upon which the curved bracket is mounted. The cross has a brass centre, and four tapered wooden arms, completely enclosed in thin iron sheeting and reinforced at their intersection by brass angle brackets. The bronze plummets are suspended through holes in the arms at distances of 45 cm. from the centre of the cross. Each plummet resembles its opposite in size and shape but differs from the neighbouring ones. The actual portions discovered included all the metal parts, with a few traces of wood fibres embedded therein. The total height of the instrument is alone considered problematical.
measurements: ['nearly 2 metres long (wooden staff)', '23.4 cm (horizontal distance between the cross and bracket pivot centres)', '45 cm (from the centre of the cross to the holes in the arms for plummets)']
interpretation: A reproduction of a Roman groma, an instrument used for surveying. The reconstruction was based on fragments discovered in Pompeii and measurements and drawings provided by Dr. Della Corte. The description details modifications made to the reconstructed instrument for improved usability.
interpretation_source: M. Della Corte's article "Groma," in Monumenti Antichi, Accademia dei Lincei, Vol. XXVIII, 1922.

description: This instrument consists of a hollow brass sphere of 2½ in. diam., with vertical great circle sighting slits cut every 45° in its surface. A socket fixed to the sphere serves to connect it to a stand.
date_made: towards the end of the 17th century
interpretation: It is used like the ordinary sight-rule cross staff for setting off angles of any multiple of 45°.

description: A brass surveying instrument with two 6-in. brass sight rules fixed accurately at right angles to each other and a central screw thread for attaching it to a stand. Backsights and foresights can be taken through either rule, every vertical arm having both a slit backsight and a wire foresight.
interpretation: This type of instrument is mostly used in detail chain and offset surveying, for setting the offset rod at right angles to the chain.

description: This instrument has two mirrors fixed to the base of a cylindrical brass box, with their planes at an angle of 45° to each other. One mirror is half unsilvered for direct vision, the other half and the whole of the second mirror being silvered, to reflect rays from objects at right angles to the line of vision. A circular aperture and rectangular windows are pierced in the side of the box opposite the mirrors.
date_made: near the end of the 18th century
interpretation: Used to reflect rays from objects at right angles to the line of vision.

description: In this instrument, two right-angled reflecting prisms are mounted one upon the other, with their reflecting faces perpendicular. In using the instrument the observer takes off the cap and screws it beneath the base to serve as a handgrip. Looking at the common face of the two prisms, he views objects on his left hand through the lower prism, and those on his right through the upper. Two objects which appear in the same vertical line will be at opposite ends of a line through the instrument, perpendicular to the direction of sight.
interpretation: Used to view objects on the left and right simultaneously, with two objects appearing in the same vertical line indicating they are at opposite ends of a line through the instrument.

description: In this instrument, made probably towards the end of the 18th century, three pairs of mirrors are mounted successively in a rectangular brass box, whose sides are provided with the necessary windows. The three pairs of mirrors make angles of 22½°, 90° and 45° respectively with each other, and one mirror of each pair is left partly unsilvered for direct vision. The direct and reflected rays for each pair are thus inclined at 45°, 180° and 90° respectively.
date_made: towards the end of the 18th century
interpretation: Optical instrument with three pairs of mirrors mounted in a brass box, used for optical reflection and squaring.

description: An instrument by means of which an observer can place himself in the direct line between two objects. It consists of two mirrors set in small parallel sighting tubes connected by a longer perpendicular tube. The planes of the mirrors are perpendicular and one mirror is partly unsilvered. The observer views the front object directly through the unsilvered portion and the rear object by double reflection at the two silvered surfaces. When the images coincide, he is in the direct line between the two objects. The sighting tubes are closed by glass windows where necessary.
interpretation: An instrument that allows an observer to align themselves with two objects by using mirrors. The observer sees the front object directly and the rear object via reflection. When the two images align, the observer is positioned in the direct line between the two objects.

description: The application of the telescope and vertical arc to the alidade of a plane table took place about the same time as the corresponding addition to the theodolite. In this exhibit, made in the late 17th century, a vertical pillar fixed perpendicularly to the alidade carries the vertical semicircle and attached telescope, which can rotate about a horizontal axis in the top of the pillar. A vernier fixed to the pillar records the altitude angle of the line of sight. The alidade is 2 ft. 4 in. long by 1½ in. wide and has one edge bevelled. Over this edge, at the two extremities of the rule, are attached two plain sights, a slit backsight and a vertical wire foresight. A few inches in front of the backsight is the vertical pillar carrying the telescope axis. By means of its milled edge and a wormwheel, the socket of this pillar can be slightly rotated in azimuth, and carries the telescope with it. This serves to adjust the line of sight parallel to the bevelled edge of the rule. The semicircle has a diameter of 5 in. and is graduated in degrees up to 50° of elevation or depression. Its edge is milled and gears with a wormwheel attached to the pillar. The telescope rests in semicircular collars fixed to the diameter of the semi-circle, and is kept in place by hinged straps and screws. It has a rack-focussing objective lens of ¾ in. aperture and a fixed eyepiece tube containing a compound field lens and eyepiece with a fixed cross wire diaphragm between the two lenses of the eyepiece. A spirit level is mounted upon the telescope parallel to its axis. The vernier attached to the pillar is slightly adjustable by means of a slide and lever, and reads the vertical arc to 3 minutes.
measurements: ['2 ft. 4 in. long', '1½ in. wide', '5 in. diameter', '¾ in. aperture']
interpretation: Used for surveying, specifically for measuring angles of elevation or depression and adjusting the line of sight.

description: An early 19th century outfit comprising plane table, tripod and brass alidade. The table, which is 17 in. by 15 in. can be rotated and levelled independently of the tripod. The alidade is nearly 2 ft. long and has a detachable combined back and foresight at each extremity, the slits and wires being vertically above the bevelled edge of the ruler. Various useful scales of length are engraved upon the alidade, and the rectangular boxwood frame forming the edge of the table is graduated on both faces in half degrees and tenth-inches. This frame is detachable and serves to clamp the paper to the table. Three centres corresponding to the half-degree graduations are marked on the table proper, by which means it can be used also as a theodolite. There is a dovetailed recess beneath the table for supporting a compass box (missing in the instrument exhibited) to orient the instrument, and a small spirit level is used to level the table. The brass piece connecting the table to the tripod has a conical axis and socket, and a spherical ball and socket joint for orienting and levelling the table independently of the tripod. The latter has a brass tripod head and circular tapering legs, 4 ft. long, jointed in the middle, and fitted with brass shoes at the extremities.
measurements: ['17 in by 15 in', 'nearly 2 ft. long', '4 ft. long']
interpretation: Can be used also as a theodolite. The compass box is missing in the instrument exhibited.

description: A small outfit of modern construction suitable for rough reconnaissance and engineering surveys. The table is 17 in. by 14 in. and has its under edges removable for inserting and clamping the drawing paper. The boxwood ruler is 12 in. long and has folding metal sights at each extremity. The back of the table has a brass plate, recessed to receive the knob of the bolt clamping it to the tripod. A small circular spirit level is used to level the table, the slope of the tripod legs being changed to effect this. A small trough compass with a 3-in. needle is provided for orienting the table. The bevelled edges of the alidade are divided in scales of 6 and 8 inches to the mile, to read 10 yd. on each scale. The sights consist of a slit backsight and strip foresight, each vertically above the centre line of the alidade.
measurements: ['17 in. by 14 in.', '12 in. long', '3-in. needle']
interpretation: Suitable for rough reconnaissance and engineering surveys.

description: A type of modern plane table outfit with telescopic alidade, suitable for topographical surveys of a comparatively high degree of precision, is here exhibited. Similar outfits have been extensively employed by the topographers of the U.S. Geological Survey. The table is 30 in. by 24 in., and is carefully made in sections to preserve its shape. Brass screw pins fitting into sockets at the corners and middle of the sides are used for fastening the drawing paper to the table, which is slightly recessed at these points to allow the heads of the pins to be flush with the upper surface of the board and thus permit the alidade to slide freely over the pins. The board is connected to the tripod by means of a Johnson quick-levelling socket, which permits it to be easily levelled and rotated in azimuth independently of the tripod. Two butterfly nuts control these movements of levelling and rotation, and, when tightened, clamp the table rigidly to the tripod. This latter has three split legs, 4 ft. long, attached by bolts to the metal tripod head and terminating in metal shoes. Any point on the sketch can be set vertically above the corresponding station point, after the instrument is levelled, by means of the wooden plumbing arm which consists of two pieces so jointed and marked at the joint that, when the upper piece is set flat on the table, with its point over the point on the sketch, and the joint clamped with its two marks coincident, the metal hook at the end of the second arm lies vertically beneath the point. The plumb-bob is suspended from this hook and the table moved until it lies over the station point. A flat 4-in. square metal plate, upon which are mounted two mutually perpendicular spirit levels and a central compass box with a 3-in. needle and ring divided in degrees, is used for levelling and orienting the table. The alidade consists of a flat brass ruler 20 in. long by 4 in. wide, having one edge bevelled and a central pillar projecting vertically from its upper face and supporting the telescope and attached vertical circle, and the fixed vernier for reading this latter. The vertical circle has a diameter of 4.5 in., and is divided on silver to half degrees, read by the vernier to single minutes. It is fixed with the telescope to the horizontal axis, which can rotate within a socket fixed to the vertical pillar. A tangent clamp and slow motion screw is fitted to this axis and connected to the vernier. The telescope is of the pattern usually fixed to 5-in. transit theodolites. It has a rack-focussing objective lens of 1.2 in. aperture and 8 in. focal length, and a rack-focussing eyepiece magnifying 20 diameters. The fixed diaphragm has two horizontal stadia wires as well as the usual cross wires.
measurements: ['30 in. by 24 in.', '4 ft. long', '4-in. square', '3-in. needle', '20 in. long by 4 in. wide', '4.5 in. diameter', '5-in.', '1.2 in. aperture', '8 in. focal length']
interpretation: A type of modern plane table outfit with telescopic alidade, suitable for topographical surveys of a comparatively high degree of precision. Similar outfits have been extensively employed by the topographers of the U.S. Geological Survey.

description: The “Vielmesser” or Polymeter, invented by R. Jähns in 1873, is an early example of a plane table alidade adapted to measure the distance, altitude, and azimuth of a point simultaneously. It is mounted upon a horizontal plane table, and used in conjunction with a tacheometric staff of constant interval, set vertically at the distant station.
interpretation: An early example of a plane table alidade adapted to measure the distance, altitude, and azimuth of a point simultaneously. Used in conjunction with a tacheometric staff.

description: A square brass plate with an engraved circle graduated in degrees over which moves an index arm carrying a small compass box.
interpretation: Probably used for plotting the bearings of objects taken with a circumferentor.

description: A brass surveying compass with
interpretation: This instrument is typical of the surveyor's compass previous to the invention of Kater's mirror compass or Schmalkalder's prismatic compass. Here the position of the needle upon the graduated compass ring, which is fixed, cannot be read at the same time as the object is viewed through the sights. Consequently it is necessary to use a stand to support the compass, and a socket is attached to the base of the wooden case for this purpose. The fixed compass ring is graduated in degrees continuously from 0° to 360° in a counter-clockwise direction. The slit backsight and wire foresight are fixed to the compass box at the 0° and 180° respectively. When the object is sighted, the reading of the S. end of the needle upon the graduated ring gives the correct magnetic bearing. These latter can be folded down upon the face of the compass for transport, and a recess is provided in the lid of the wooden case for their reception. This lid, on being closed, depresses a pin which lifts the needle from its pivot and clamps it against the glass cover.

description: This compass, probably made about the end of the 18th century, differs only in minor details from the adjacent one made by Dollond. It has a 3½ in. compass ring graduated in degrees, mounted in a brass case to which sights can be fitted, and which has a threaded socket for attaching the instrument to a stand when taking bearings. The graduations are numbered every 10° in quadrants, with the 0° at the N. and S. points. Opposite these points are sliding sockets in the outer case. The two sights, each having a slit and a wire for use as backsight and foresight respectively, are mounted in these sockets when in use, or fitted within the lid of the compass case for transport. The sights are 3 in. long. The compass needle is provided with a lifting lever actuated by a pin which is depressed when the lid is fitted on the case, but has no clamping arrangement.
date_made: about the end of the 18th century
interpretation: Used for taking bearings.

description: The mirror attachment to the eye lens here shown was invented by Capt. Kater at the beginning of the 19th century, and enables the observer to view the graduations of the horizontal compass ring at the same time as he takes a sight. The compass ring is fixed to the rotating needle and is so graduated in half-degrees consecutively from 0° to 360° that correct bearings are read off immediately. The usual slit backsight and wire foresight are fixed to the compass box at a distance apart of 5 in. A small pin fixed in the case vertically beneath the backsight serves as fiducial mark, and its position on the graduated scale is seen through the mirror very clearly when the instrument is held about one foot away from the eye. The foresight can be folded down upon the top of the case, and the compass card and needle are thereby automatically lifted from the pivot and clamped.
interpretation: Enables the observer to view the graduations of the horizontal compass ring at the same time as he takes a sight. The compass ring is fixed to the rotating needle and is so graduated in half-degrees consecutively from 0° to 360° that correct bearings are read off immediately. The foresight can be folded down upon the top of the case, and the compass card and needle are thereby automatically lifted from the pivot and clamped.

description: The reflecting mirror used by Captain Kater for viewing the graduated compass ring was superseded in 1812 by the application of Schmalkalder's prismatic eyepiece to the compass. By this means the observer can read the bearing and sight the object simultaneously, and can thus dispense with a stand for the instrument. The compass card is 2½ in. in diameter, and is fixed to the magnetic needle. It is graduated in consecutive half-degrees from 0° to 360° in a clockwise direction, the N. end of the needle being under the 180° mark. The diagonal prism is attached to the plate which has a slit serving as backsight, and is ground convex on one perpendicular face so as to magnify the image of the graduated card seen by reflection at its inclined face, which is silvered. This backsight plate is jointed to the compass box, and can be folded down when the instrument is not in use. The foresight consists of a vertical wire fixed in a frame diametrically opposite the back-sight, and similarly jointed to the base so as to fold down when not in use. Mirrors and coloured glasses are attached to the sights for taking bearing upon the sun and other celestial objects. A lever is provided for lifting the needle from its pivot and locking the compass card when desired, and there is a steadying pin underneath the foresight for damping the oscillations of the card.
interpretation: For this reason the prismatic compass has come into general use for rapid reconnaissance surveys.

description: This instrument, constructed in the early part of the 19th century, is essentially a combined theodolite and prismatic compass. The telescopic alidade, which carries the prismatic eyepiece and a vernier underneath this, can be rotated about the vertical axis independently of the compass box, the instrument thus acting as a theodolite—or can be rotated together with the compass ring, in which case it fulfills the functions of a prismatic compass. The compass ring is graduated directly to 20' in a clockwise direction and is read by vernier to single minutes. The instrument is attached to a stand by means of a ball and socket arrangement, and can be levelled independently of the stand by four screws which engage in threads in the socket and press against the vertical axis. There is also a tangent clamp and slow motion screw for rotating the whole instrument in azimuth, whilst a circular rack and pinion inside the compass box serves to rotate the alidade independently. This is actuated by the screw projecting beneath the compass. The telescope carries a small spirit level, and is screwed at the eyepiece end to a brass plate hinged to a sliding piece, whilst it rests at the objective end in a Y-piece fixed to another sliding piece. These two sliding pieces terminate at their lower ends in screws, which work in threaded plates screwed to the compass box. Thus the telescope can be elevated at either end with respect to the compass box and can be adjusted so as to be horizontal. It is focussed by sliding the objective lens.
interpretation: Combined theodolite and prismatic compass. Used for surveying.

description: The quadrant attached to this instrument, which is in other respects similar to the Schmalcalder prismatic compass, enables it to be used for measuring altitudes as well as taking magnetic bearings. The quadrant has separate sights and a small spirit level fixed to a movable radial arm. A mark engraved on the outer end of this arm registers the altitude upon the graduated arc of the quadrant when the arm is horizontal and the sights are directed upon the distant object. A small spirit level is fixed to the bottom of the case inside and serves to set the compass horizontal. The altitude quadrant has a radius of 2 in. and is attached to the wire foresight of the compass. It is graduated in degrees from 0° to 90°, the radius corresponding to the former being parallel to the compass plane, and carrying the supplementary sights, a pin-hole back-sight and a cross-wire foresight, for determining altitudes. Mirrors and coloured glasses are attached to the two compass sights for taking bearings on high objects such as the sun.
interpretation: Enables measurement of altitudes as well as taking magnetic bearings. Used for measuring altitudes and taking magnetic bearings.

description: In this instrument, constructed about the middle of the 19th century, the method of lifting and locking the compass card is similar to that employed by Schmalcalder. The card is graduated in degrees, in two sets numbered consecutively in the clockwise sense from 0° to 180°. There are no mirrors or coloured glasses for celestial observations.
interpretation: The diameter of the compass ring is 2½ in. and it can be read by estimation to the nearest 10'.

description: This instrument, which was made about the middle of the 19th century, differs very little from those made by Schmalcalder about 30 years previously. The compass card is not graduated continuously from 0° to 360°, but in two sets of 180°, both in the clockwise sense. It reads directly to half-degrees, and by estimation to 10'. The compass card is lifted and clamped by folding down the foresight. The usual mirror and coloured glasses are provided for observing celestial objects. The eye prism is adjustable for focussing, and there is a steadying pin under the foresight for damping the oscillations of the compass needle.
interpretation: Used for surveying. The compass card is not graduated continuously from 0° to 360°, but in two sets of 180°, both in the clockwise sense. It reads directly to half-degrees, and by estimation to 10'. The compass card is lifted and clamped by folding down the foresight. The eye prism is adjustable for focussing, and there is a steadying pin under the foresight for damping the oscillations of the compass needle.

description: Except for the arrangement to lift and lock the compass card, this instrument differs very little from those made by Schmalcalder nearly a century previously. The compass card, prismatic eyepiece, steadying pin, etc., remain the same, but the eyepiece is here arranged so that the eye must be nearer the slit for focussing than in Schmalcalder's instruments, whilst the folding down of the foresight upon the compass automatically lifts and clamps the card. The card is graduated in half-degrees in the usual clockwise sense. Both the sights can be folded down, and the prismatic eyepiece can be adjusted for focussing the gradua-tions. There are the usual mirrors and coloured glasses for taking bearings of celestial objects. A socket is rigidly fixed to the base of the compass box for attaching it to a stand. When the compass is so mounted, bearings can be taken to within 15', and estimated to the nearest 5'.
interpretation: Used for taking bearings of celestial objects. Allows for precise bearing readings when mounted on a stand.

description: A modern type of compass specially designed for rough surveying and for night marching upon a given bearing, previously set off on the edge of the compass. It has a hair foresight upon the hinged lid, and a slit backsight upon the hinged mounting carrying the prismatic reader. Various marks in luminous paint upon the lid, cover plate and dial of the compass are used in night marching. The compass has a spring damping pin for checking the oscillations of the dial as well as a lifting pin for locking it when not in use. The luminous marks on the lid are at the extremities of the hair foresight. The glass cover plate of the compass box also has a luminous mark and can be independently rotated so as to set this mark at any angle to the sight line. The angle so set is measured by means of an index mark on the cover in conjunction with the graduated edge of the compass box. This is set to the bearing upon which it is desired to march, and the cover plate locked by means of a spring catch which engages in the milled edge of the plate. The dial of the compass, which is fixed to the magnetic needle and pivoted so as to rotate freely, has a luminous arrow marked above the north pole of the magnet. When the compass is turned until the luminous mark on the cover plate lies above the luminous arrow on the dial, the luminous marks at the extremity of the hair line on the lid point in the direction it is desired to march. For surveying purposes the compass dial is graduated in degrees round its edge, the numbers being inverted so as to appear upright when seen through the prism, and so arranged that the correct bearing of the line of sight is read directly through the prism. There is a supplementary set of numbered graduations every 5° for direct reading without using the prism. A ring is hinged to the box to steady it when taking bearings, and a lever on the lid automatically actuates the lifting pin when the lid is closed.
interpretation: Specially designed for rough surveying and for night marching upon a given bearing. Used for setting off bearings, checking oscillations of the dial, and locking it when not in use. Luminous marks facilitate night marching. Dial is graduated in degrees for direct reading of bearing. Supplementary graduations allow reading without a prism. A hinged ring steadies the compass when taking bearings. A lever actuates the lifting pin when the lid is closed.

description: This instrument combines the advantages of prismatic reading with the rapid and accurate setting afforded by nearly floating the compass card in a liquid, which reduces the friction of the pivot and rapidly damps the motion of the card. The dial can be illuminated for night reading by means of an electric bulb fixed beneath the transparent base of the compass box. A socket attached to the base enables the compass to be mounted upon the tripod exhibited with it. The compass card has a diameter of 2·5 in. and is graduated in degrees, read by an internal index point mounted beneath the centre of the prismatic reader. The card carries two cylindrical magnetic needles fixed below it with their axes parallel, and has a central buoyant chamber resting upon the pivot. The card, needles and pivot are enclosed in a watertight chamber filled with a mixture of water and alcohol, which has a low freezing point. The card just rests upon the pivot, without pressing much on it, so that there is little frictional resistance to its rotation, and its motion is nearly "critically damped" by the liquid so that it takes up its new setting after rotation within a few seconds. The prismatic reader has a V-shaped backsight used with the long foresight bracket upon which is a travelling foresight. Owing to the freedom of the needle from vibration, the reading can be taken to the nearest fifth degree. The electric bulb serving to illuminate the dial for night reading is operated by a plug switch and a battery of two small cells, carried in the leather case used for transporting the compass.
interpretation: Combines prismatic reading with rapid and accurate setting by floating the compass card in liquid to reduce pivot friction and damp card motion. The dial can be illuminated for night reading. The compass can be mounted on a tripod. The card is graduated in degrees. The card has two cylindrical magnetic needles and a central buoyant chamber. The card, needles, and pivot are enclosed in a watertight chamber filled with a water and alcohol mixture. The card rests lightly on the pivot, minimizing frictional resistance and allowing rapid setting. The prismatic reader has a V-shaped backsight. Readings can be taken to the nearest fifth degree due to the needle's freedom from vibration. The electric bulb for illumination is operated by a plug switch and battery, carried in a leather case.

description: In this type of military compass, invented by Capt. Burnier about 1850, the graduated edge of the compass ring, which is fixed to the needle and rotates with it, is perpendicular to the plane of the needle. The bearing of the sighting thread can therefore be viewed at the same time as a sight is taken. A weighted disc is mounted parallel to the compass ring, and has a similar graduated edge. On clamping the compass ring and bringing the planes of both rings vertical, the disc is unclamped and serves as a clinometer. Either ring is viewed through a cylindrical eye lens, which closes the brass case and is about 2 cm. distant from the graduated edges. A double-jointed socket attached to the base of the case permits the instrument to be rotated in a vertical or a horizontal plane upon a stick stand, and serves as a support for holding the instrument when no stand is used. The compass ring is graduated in degrees continuously from 0° to 360°, and the magnetic bearing of the object sighted is read off directly. The clinometer ring is likewise graduated in degrees, and is weighted at the 90° portion. The usual folding slit and wire sights are attached to the top of the case, and are easily viewed simultaneously with the graduated rings when the instrument is held about a foot from the eye. A wire mounted within the case near the graduated edges in the plane of these two sights serves as fiducial mark. The whole instrument is compact and serviceable, and is in general use on the Continent for military and reconnaissance surveys.
measurements: ['4 cm. diameter', '2 mm. deep', '2 cm. distant']
interpretation: Used for routine land surveying in the late 19th century.
interpretation_source: Laussedat's "Recherches sur les Instruments Topographiques," Vol. I, p. 306

description: These two examples of Casella's "Pocket Altazimuth," or combined compass and clinometer, illustrate the experimental stages of development of the instrument, which is represented in its modern form by an adjacent exhibit. Each instrument consists of two graduated aluminium rings separately mounted upon pivots along the axis of a single cylindrical metal box, which is closed by glass faces. A magnetic needle is fixed to one ring, which acts as a compass to determine azimuths, whilst the other ring is loaded at one point and serves as a plummet clinometer for measuring altitude angles. When not in use, each ring can be lifted from its pivots and clamped by means of a lever actuated by a sliding knob. In one instrument the graduated edges of the rings are read by means of two small telescopes, one for each ring, mounted on the metal box; a thin wire is stretched across the box between the telescopes and the rings and defines the index line, or line of sight. In the other instrument, a single telescope can be fitted so as to read either ring alternately, and also to sight upon a distant object. This telescope has a single objective lens and a dual eyepiece, comprising a lens for sighting on the distant object and a prism for reading the graduations upon the upper face of the compass or clinometer ring. In both instruments the rings are graduated in degrees, and a flat footing is attached to the box so that it can be placed upon any surface of which the inclination is to be measured.
interpretation: Used for measuring altitude angles and determining azimuths. Illustrates experimental stages of development of a combined compass and clinometer.

description: This is a compact form of combined telescopic compass and clinometer of a design embodying improvements due to Sir Francis Galton, F.R.S. Either magnetic bearings or altitude angles can be measured independently, but not simultaneously, with it. It consists of two graduated rings, separately pivoted within a cylindrical case, having glass-covered ends parallel to the planes of the two rings. One of the rings is graduated at the 32 points of the compass, and has a diametrical magnetic needle whose centre rests on the pivot. The other ring is loaded at one part of its circumference and is pivoted to the case on each side. It is graduated in degrees, numbered in quadrants, with the zero point opposite the centre of gravity of the load. Both rings have a diameter of $1rac{1}{4}$ in., the external diameter of the cylindrical case being $2rac{1}{2}$ in. The compass ring only moves when its plane is horizontal, the clinometer ring when its plane is vertical. Each ring is clamped when its plane is in use, and is read by the position of an index mark on the cylindrical case. The latter carries a telescope, whose axis is parallel to the ends of the cylinder and passes through the line of pivots of the ring. The telescope has its objective tube and eyepiece tube separately fixed to the case, the latter being partly without and partly within the case, and having a slide-focussing eyepiece. A hair line is stretched across the case just behind the objective lens. A base piece for supporting the instrument is attached to the case, with its plane base parallel to the axis of the telescope. There is also a central threaded hole in the base for fixing it to a tripod. A damping spring is provided for use with the compass ring. The complete instrument weighs only 8 oz.
measurements: ['$1\x0crac{1}{4}$ in. diameter', '$2\x0crac{1}{2}$ in. external diameter', '8 oz.']
interpretation: This is a compact form of combined telescopic compass and clinometer. It is particularly suitable for very approximate reconnaissance surveying.

description: This is a modern example of a French type of surveying compass, with an eccentrically mounted telescope, used on the Continent on minor work. The compass is fixed in a flat, rectangular wooden box, to one side of which is attached the telescope, rotating about an axis fixed perpendicularly to this side. The whole instrument can rotate in the plane of the compass ring, which can itself be varied by means of a ball-and-socket joint.
interpretation: Used on the Continent on minor work.

description: The date of this instrument is indicated by the allowance for magnetic declination on the compass ring, on which the meridian is engraved at the point $10^{\circ}$ E. of N. This corresponds to the year 1590, in England.
interpretation: Allowance for magnetic declination on the compass ring.

description: This instrument probably dates from the early 17th century. It consists of a brass circle, graduated in degrees, having two pairs of fixed sights along perpendicular diameters, and a movable alidade fitted with pointers at each end. It can be set upon a stand for measuring angles in any plane, or suspended from a ring attached to the circumference for taking altitudes.
interpretation: This instrument probably dates from the early 17th century. It can be set upon a stand for measuring angles in any plane, or suspended from a ring attached to the circumference for taking altitudes.

description: In this instrument, which was probably made in the early 17th century, only one pair of fixed sights is provided, defining a horizontal line when the instrument is suspended from the ring attached to its circumference. The movable alidade carries the usual slit sights and terminates in pointers. There is a circular ring on one arm of the instrument which probably supported a magnetic compass. The circle is graduated in degrees in four sets from 0° to 90°. On the back of the instrument is attached a socket with a fixing screw for receiving the head of a stand. The suspension ring is specially jointed to permit the plane of the circle to hang freely vertical.
interpretation: Used for surveying. In this instrument, only one pair of fixed sights is provided, defining a horizontal line when the instrument is suspended from the ring attached to its circumference. The suspension ring is specially jointed to permit the plane of the circle to hang freely vertical.

description: This instrument consists of a graphometer whose alidades are fitted with points to serve as compasses, and have various scales engraved on them corresponding to those usually found on sectors, and used in measuring lines, setting off angles, taking weights of spherical shot, etc. A small magnetic compass is attached to the junction of the two alidades. There is no evidence that this instrument was fitted to a stand, and it was presumably employed in conjunction with a plane table, on which it rested when angles were observed.
interpretation: Used for measuring lines, setting off angles, taking weights of spherical shot, etc. Assumed to be employed in conjunction with a plane table.

description: This is a 17th-century theodolite of Continental design, the alidade being mounted near the edge of the circle and connected to a centrally mounted parallel index arm used to read the circle. The circle has a diameter of 6 1/4 in., and a 2 1/4-in. compass box is centrally fixed above the movable index arm. The circle is divided on its outer edge into 360 degrees, but has a concentric circle, of 5 in. diam., divided into 320 parts, also read by the diametral index arm. Each circle is divided into octants and the divisions of each octant numbered in the clockwise sense from 0 to 45 on the outer circle and from 0 to 40 on the inner. The outer octants are successively designated by the letters T, G, L, S, O, A, P, M, which are the initial letters of the old Italian names for the compass points. The inner octants each commence at the central points of the outer ones, and are named Septentrio, Aquilo, Solanus, Eurus, Auster, Africus, Favonius, and Chaurus respectively, which are the old Latin titles for the winds corresponding to the cardinal points. The central index arm has bevelled edges at each extremity for reading the divisions. The alidade is about 9 in. long and has folding combined back and foresights at each end. It rotates with the index arm about the axis of the circle. The compass box, fixed to the circle above the index arm, has its base divided into octants, but no subdivisions.
measurements: ['6 1/4 in. diameter', '2 1/4-in. compass box', '5 in. diam.', '9 in. long']
interpretation: Used for reading the circle, with divisions numbered and named according to compass points and winds. The alidade has folding combined back and foresights for use.

description: This instrument is a combined graphometer, or surveying semicircle, and clinometer. The graduated semicircle can be detached from the frame and used as a protractor for plotting the angles in the field. A compass is attached to the frame for orienting the instrument, and the whole is attached to a stand by means of a double-knuckled joint, permitting it to be set in any plane. It can also rotate as a whole in that plane. The semicircle has one fixed and one movable alidade. The semicircle is graduated in degrees, and has a diagonal scale enabling it to read to 5′. The compass ring is graduated in degrees. On the back of the plate carrying it is a simple quadrant pendulum clinometer, also graduated in degrees, and provided with “Umbra Versa” and “Umbra Recta” scales for measuring heights. The clinometer is attached to an alidade, which is connected to the semicircle by a spring clip and can be disconnected for taking altitudes.
interpretation: This is particularly interesting as showing that the much simpler vernier system was not yet in general use, although invented over 30 years previously.

description: This instrument has a radius of 6 in. and is graduated in half-degrees. By means of a vernier arc covering 31' and divided into 60 parts, angles can be measured to the nearest half-minute. The index arm carrying this vernier is pivoted at the centre of the quadrant and carries three folding sights, one at its centre and the other two at the ends of its arc. Two similar sights are fixed at the ends of the quadrant arc. The quadrant is attached to a socket for fixing it upon a stand by a ball and socket joint permitting it to be set in any plane, including the vertical.
interpretation: Angles can be measured to the nearest half-minute.

description: A very fine example of an early theodolite, which has a circle of 12 in. diam., graduated every 10' and read by a vernier on the alidade to 1'. A 2-in. compass is fixed at the centre of the circle and has its ring divided in degrees.
interpretation: An early theodolite with precise graduations and readings.

description: This instrument consists of one fixed and one movable alidade, each provided with sights, intersecting each other at the centre of a semicircle graduated to read half-degrees. The whole is mounted upon a ball and socket joint.
interpretation: can be used to measure angles in any plane.

description: This example was constructed in 1686, and exhibits many characteristics of that period. The alidade plate is square, and can be detached from its support and employed as a protractor. On it are engraved three concentric graduated circles, of diameters 8 in., 7 in. and 3 in. The outer circle is divided in degrees, with two sets of numberings. The central circle is a "Scala altimetra," or tangent scale, for measuring heights, and the inner circle is divided into 32 parts corresponding to the points of the compass. The movable alidade carries a 2 1/4-in. compass box, and is pivoted at the centre of the plate. At one end is a vernier arc which moves over the outer graduated circle, and reads this to single minutes, the 60 divisions of the vernier extending over 61°. The fixed and movable sights have circular apertures, with vertical slits above their centres, and are carved and ornamentally engraved. Two edges of the square plate are parallel to the two fixed sights, which can be folded down upon the plate when not in use. The conical socket for attaching the instrument to its stand has a ball and socket joint permitting the alidade plate to be set in any plane, including the vertical. It is kept in position by the friction of the joint, there being no clamping screw. The compass plate is graduated in degrees, numbered left and right from the N. and S. points from 0° to 90°. A compass rose indicating the 32 main points is engraved inside the circle. On the back of the alidade plate are engraved a clinometer scale for use of artillery, and the inscription "Jacobus Lussorg Mutinensis Faciebat Romae A° 1686", with the arms and coronet of the Duke of Modena.
interpretation: The alidade plate can be detached from its support and employed as a protractor. The central circle is a "Scala altimetra," or tangent scale, for measuring heights. On the back of the alidade plate are engraved a clinometer scale for use of artillery.

description: This early 18th-century example is typical of the circumferentor of that period. It is a combined theodolite—having a graduated limb of 11 in. diam., reading by vernier to 5'—and compass, with a 6-in. needle reading to half-degrees. The theodolite limb is graduated in single degrees in the clockwise sense from 0° to 360°, and carries a pair of fixed sights, each with a slit and window for sighting both ways, at its 0° and 180° marks. The movable alidade, carrying a similar pair of sights, has a vernier at one end reading to 5' and a central fiducial mark at the other end. The compass box is fixed to this alidade with its N. point above the zero of the vernier. The compass ring is graduated consecutively in half-degrees from 0° to 360° in a counter-clockwise sense, so that the position of the N. end of the needle gives the magnetic bearing of the alidade sights. Both pairs of sights are employed when the instrument is used as a theodolite, but only the alidade sights when taking magnetic bearings. The instrument is mounted upon a tripod when in use.
interpretation: A combined theodolite and compass used for surveying. The compass needle indicates the magnetic bearing of the alidade sights, and both sets of sights are used when operating as a theodolite.

description: This early 18th-century instrument has a 10 1/4-in. graduated circle, reading by vernier to 5'. The vernier is attached at one end of the movable alidade, to which is also fixed the compass ring, which has a 6-in. diam. and is graduated in degrees. The sights on the movable alidade, and those fixed on the large circle are each fitted with both slits and vertical wires, and can be used either as back or fore sights. They are sufficiently high to permit the measurement of angles in the horizontal plane, and the whole instrument is designed for such measurements, and not for determining angles in any plane. The outer circle is graduated in degrees, and reads from 0° to 360° in a clockwise sense. The fixed sights are attached at the 0° and 180° points. The compass ring has two sets of graduations, one set reading degrees from 0° to 360° in a counter-clockwise sense, the other set giving every 10° only from 0° to 90° in each quadrant, the N. and S. points being the zero points. The eight main points of the compass are likewise indicated. The whole instrument fits upon a stand by means of a socket fixed on the back of the large circle.
interpretation: Designed for measurements in the horizontal plane, and not for determining angles in any plane.

description: An early 18th-century example of the graphometer, or surveying semicircle, much used in France in preference to the English theodolite. It has a diameter of 11 in. and is graduated in degrees, read by vernier on the rotating alidade to 5'. A 3-in. compass, with its ring divided in degrees, is mounted eccentrically on the semicircle. Combined slit and wire sights are fixed at opposite ends of the diameter of the semicircle, and their orientation determined by means of the compass. A similar pair of sights is attached to the alidade, which rotates about the centre of the semicircle, and has bevelled verniers at each end. The axis of the semicircle terminates below in a spherical ball and socket arrangement for mounting the instrument on a tripod and setting its semicircle in any plane. The graduations of the semicircle are numbered both ways from 0° to 180°, those of the compass ring in four quadrants, with the zeros at the N. and S. points. The compass needle is supplied with a lifting needle for clamping it to the top of its box when transporting the instrument.
interpretation: This is an early 18th-century example of the graphometer, or surveying semicircle, much used in France in preference to the English theodolite.

description: In this instrument, which was constructed towards the end of the 18th century, the compass has a diameter of $1rac{1}{2}$ in. and is graduated only at the eight cardinal points. It is arranged for a magnetic variation of 16° W. The main circle has a diameter of 6 in. and is graduated in degrees, numbered both ways from 0° to 180° from the diameter underneath the pair of fixed sights. The alidade carrying the movable sights is fixed to the compass box and rotates with it about the vertical axis. The compass needle is pivoted upon a plate fixed to the horizontal circle. There are no verniers, but only bevelled reading edges, on the alidade, and the sights are not suited for sighting both ways, but consist of a simple slit backsight on one end of the alidade and a wire foresight at the other end. The graduated circle can be set in any desired plane by means of a ball and socket joint connecting it to the stand.

description: This instrument, made about the end of the 18th century, is a good example of the circumferentor of that period. It has two small spirit levels fixed in the base of the compass box for setting the instrument horizontal. The 6-in. circle is graduated in degrees in the clockwise sense from 0° to 360°, and read by the vernier at one end of the alidade to 3'. The compass ring, with a 4-in. needle, is graduated in degrees in the counter-clockwise sense from 0° to 360°. Both fixed and movable sights are provided with slits and windows for sighting in either direction. The small spirit levels upon the base of the compass box were not considered necessary by the makers, but were provided owing to the wishes of many surveyors. The socket attached to the base does not appear to have the customary screw for clamping the instrument to its tripod.

interpretation: Used for routine land surveying.

description: This instrument, dating from the early part of the 18th century, illustrates a fundamental stage in the development of the theodolite. Upon the alidade of a “common theodolite” of the type very generally used in the 17th century, is mounted a fixed graduated vertical arc. A telescope upon which is fixed a longitudinal spirit level, carries a vernier arm which traverses the graduated arc as the telescope rotates, and thus measures the altitude of the object sighted at the same time as the alidade measures its azimuth. The horizontal circle in this instrument has a diameter of 10 in. and is graduated in degrees, numbered from 0° to 260° in the clockwise sense. The alidade has a vernier at one extremity reading the horizontal circle to 5'. A 5-in. compass box is mounted centrally upon this alidade and gives magnetic bearings in single degrees. The vertical arc is graduated in degrees, with the zero at the point vertically beneath the telescope axis, and reads by vernier to 10'. Altitude angles up to 40° of elevation or depression can be measured. The telescope has a focal length of 8 in., an aperture of 1 in., and an erecting eyepiece with a simple cross-wire diaphragm. The spirit level is rigidly attached to the telescope tube. The instrument is attached to its tripod by means of a socket fixed beneath the centre of the horizontal circle.

The horizontal circle  is graduated in degrees, numbered from 0° to 260° in the clockwise sense. The alidade has a vernier at one extremity reading the horizontal circle to 5'. A 5-in. compass box is mounted centrally upon this alidade and gives magnetic bearings in single degrees. The vertical arc is graduated in degrees, with the zero at the point vertically beneath the telescope axis, and reads by vernier to 10'. interpretation: Among the early 18th-century makers of surveying instruments, Sisson is generally regarded as the most expert, and his design of altazimuth theodolite, of which the instrument exhibited is typical, remained the standard until Ramsden’s time. This example has a $4rac{1}{2}$-in. horizontal circle, graduated in degrees and read by three symmetrically placed verniers to 6'. The vertical arc, reading angles up to 70° of elevation or depression, has a radius of 2 in. and is similarly graduated and read by a single vernier centrally placed on the horizontal vernier plate. Both circles have toothed edges, in which engage pinion wheels, the motion of rotation being effected by turning these pinions. The telescope is attached above the vertical arc by screw bearings which permit it to be adjusted to sight horizontally when the vertical arc reads zero. A small spirit level fixed above the telescope, and a smaller one rigidly joined to the vertical arc enable this adjustment to be effected. The horizontal axis of rotation of the vertical arc and telescope rests on standards projecting from the central plate carrying the three horizontal vernier arms. To one of these is attached a clamp and screw which regulates the friction between the movable vernier plate and the fixed horizontal circle. In another vernier arm is fixed the axis of rotation of the pinion wheel which engages in the teeth of the horizontal circle. Beneath the horizontal circle is screwed a compass box of 4 in. diameter. The compass ring is not graduated, but has index marks beneath the o° and the 180° graduations of the horizontal circle. This enables the instrument to be oriented. The conical socket for attaching the theodolite to a staff, or to a levelling device consisting of two parallel plates and four levelling screws, is fixed beneath the compass box. The telescope has a fixed objective of $rac{3}{4}$-in. aperture, and a sliding Huygens ocular, with a simple fixed cross-wire diaphragm.

description: The vertical arc is fixed to the alidade, and the vernier to the telescope. The 8-in. horizontal circle is graduated in degrees and read to 5' by means of a vernier scale on the alidade. The vertical arc has a radius of 3 in. and is graduated in degrees up to 50° on each side of the zero. It also is read to 5' by its vernier. The 4-in. compass mounted on the alidade is graduated in degrees in the counter clockwise sense. The telescope of 10-in. focal length and 0.5-in. aperture, has a single lens, draw-focussing eyepiece and a simple cross-wire diaphragm. Spirit levels are fixed on the telescope tube and the base of the compass box. The two parallel plates for fixing the instrument to its tripod are connected by four levelling screws and a spherical joint.

description: In this theodolite, the alidade is replaced by a circular plate carrying two widely separated standards upon which is mounted the horizontal axis of rotation. The vertical semicircle is fixed to this axis, whilst the vernier is fixed on the circular plate. The telescope rests in jointed rings attached above the semicircle. The 7-in. horizontal circle is graduated in degrees, and read by a vernier scale on the alidade plate to 5'. The vertical semicircle is of the same diam. and is graduated in degrees on one side, with scales of feet and links on the other. It is also read by vernier to 5', and can measure angles up to 60° on either side of the vertical. The compass fixed on the alidade plate has a diam. of 3 in. and is graduated in degrees. The telescope, of 7-in. focal length and 0.5-in. aperture, has a single-lens, draw-focussing eyepiece. A spirit level is fixed by adjustable screws beneath the telescope tube, parallel to its axis. The horizontal circle is attached by a clamping screw to the upper of two parallel plates, which are connected to each other by four levelling screws and a spherical joint.

description: This instrument, made towards the end of the 18th century, illustrates the many improvements in design due to Ramsden. The alidade and horizontal plates have their graduated edges bevelled to facilitate reading, and are supported by accurately made conical axes. A tangent clamp and slow-motion screw control the horizontal motion, and the ball and socket joint connecting the two parallel plates of the levelling attachment is very solidly and accurately constructed. The telescope has an achromatic, rack-focussing objective lens of 8·5-in. focal length and 1-in. aperture, and an erecting eyepiece. It rests in Y-s attached to the ends of the vertical semicircle, which has a radius of 3 in. and is graduated on one face in half-degrees. This arc is read by a fixed vernier to 1′, and used to measure angles of elevation or depression up to 60°. The 7-in. horizontal circle is divided in half-degrees and read by two opposing verniers to 1′. The compass box, has a 3-in. ring graduated in degrees and a sensitive needle which can be lifted from its pivot by means of a lever when required. The box is mounted between the telescope standards upon an adjustable stage, which is connected to the horizontal vernier plate by capstan-headed screws. Spirit levels are mounted on the telescope and the vernier plate.

description: This instrument was made in the early part of the 19th century, and in details resembles the adjacent example made by Ramsden. There is, however, a supplementary telescope used for keeping the back-set station in view. The horizontal circle and vertical semicircle have diameters of 7 in., are graduated in half-degrees, and read by vernier to single minutes. Both are rotated by rack and pinion movements. There is a tangent clamp and slow-motion screw to the horizontal circle. The telescope rests in Y-s attached to the vertical arc, and moves with this. The standards supporting the horizontal axis of rotation are fixed upon an adjustable stage, attached to the alidade plate by three capstan-headed screws. This stage carries the compass box, which has a 3-in. ring, graduated in degrees. The two telescopes are of precisely similar optical construction. Each has a 7-in. achromatic objective, with a 1·2-in. aperture, and a rack and pinion-focussing mechanism. Their eyepieces are erecting and consist of four lenses, with a draw-focussing mechanism. The supplementary telescope has a full azimuthal motion round the vertical axis of the instrument, and a small altitude movement. The construction of the parallel plate mounting is of the usual Ramsden type, with four levelling screws. There is a longitudinal spirit level fixed in adjustable bearings beneath the telescope, and two levels with their axes at right angles on the alidade plate.
interpretation: Used for surveying.

description: This instrument, although made in the middle of the 19th century, retains most of the features characterising the Ramsden type of theodolite. Tangent clamps and slow-motion screws replace the Ramsden rack and pinion movements for both horizontal and vertical circles, and small reading microscopes are provided near the verniers. The supporting standards for the horizontal axis of rotation are not mounted upon an adjustable stage, as in Ramsden’s instruments, but are fixed directly to the alidade plate. The telescope is mounted in Ys attached to the vertical arc. The eyepiece is erecting, with four lenses, and a draw-focussing mechanism. The diaphragm has one vertical and one horizontal wire. A sensitive longitudinal spirit level is fixed in adjustable bearings beneath the telescope. On the alidade there are two smaller levels at right angles to each other, and a 3-in. compass graduated in degrees. The parallel plates are of the usual Ramsden type, with four levelling screws.

description: This instrument, probably constructed about 1840, differs in many respects from the more usual Y-theodolite of the period. Its telescope is rigidly attached to the horizontal axis of rotation, which carries the vertical arc and rests in bearings upon two standards fixed to the rim of a case whose bottom forms the alidade. This case is closed at the top by a glass cover, so that the horizontal circle and compass are enclosed. Reading microscopes with prism reflectors are attached to the case for reading the verniers of the horizontal circle. Tangent clamps and slow-motion screws are fitted to both circles. The upper part of the instrument is suspended in a gimbal mounting within a hollow cylinder screwed upon the tripod plate, and can be levelled independently of the tripod by two screws threaded into the cylinder, with diametrically opposite springs. These screws press against a square nut fixed to the lower end of the axial cone which carries the horizontal circle. The 6-in. horizontal circle is graduated to 20' and read by vernier to 30''. The 5-in. vertical arc is similarly graduated and read by vernier, and has a range of 50° on either side of the zero mark. The telescope is achromatic, with a 1-in. aperture and 8-in. focal length. The objective is focussed by a rack and pinion mechanism. The eyepiece is a simple Ramsden inverting draw-focussing one, and the diaphragm has one vertical and one horizontal wire. A diagonal reflecting mirror can be attached in front of the objective for taking steep sights. There is one longitudinal adjustable spirit level attached beneath the telescope, and a parallel one fixed to the standards but no transverse level. The alidade carries a 3-in. compass, graduated in degrees.

description: The Everest pattern theodolite, although not possessing the advantage of a transit instrument, has been much used by the British and Indian Survey departments since its inception, due to Sir George (then Captain) Everest, about the year 1835. The one exhibited is a late 19th-century 5-in. model, the horizontal circle and vertical arcs being graduated to 20' and read by two opposing verniers to 30''. In the Everest type of theodolite two opposing vertical arcs are used instead of a complete vertical circle, and the horizontal axis to which the telescope and arcs are fixed, is mounted upon two short standards projecting from a central pillar, supported on the horizontal vernier plate. The vernier bracket and attached spirit level are mounted on the axis, and are clamped to one standard by opposing screws. Two perpendicular spirit levels are likewise mounted on the horizontal vernier plate. The horizontal circle has a bevelled graduated edge and a separate mounting on the vertical axis cone. Thus the vernier plate and circle have independent motions, controlled by clamps and tangent screws, for repeating azimuth angles. All verniers are provided with reading microscopes. The instrument has a tribrach mounting, the feet of the three levelling screws resting in grooves in a trivet plate and being locked therein by a spring-controlled locking plate—also a feature of the original Everest design. The telescope has a rack-focussing objective of 1·2-in. aperture and 9-in. focal length, and a slide-focussing Ramsden eyepiece. Owing to the low standards, angles of elevation beyond 30° and of depression beyond 45° cannot be measured, as the telescope then fouls the horizontal plates. The vertical arcs consequently only extend about 50° on each side of the horizontal zeros.

interpretation: Used by the British and Indian Survey departments since its inception. description: An early example of a transit theodolite. Below the horizontal circle it resembles Ramsden's Y-theodolite, but the upper part has standards sufficiently high to permit the telescope to transit at either end. Both horizontal and vertical circles are 6 in. diam., divided on silver to 10′ and read by opposing verniers to 10″. The vernier plate and horizontal circle have independent axes of rotation for repeating angles, and are bevelled at the graduations to facilitate reading. Reading microscopes are provided for both circles, and also tangent clamps and slow-motion screws, as well as a similar clamp and screw connecting the vernier plate to the horizontal circle. The axis of this circle rests in a conical socket attached to the upper of two parallel levelling plates, connected by four screws and a ball and socket joint. The vernier plate carries a single spirit level, parallel to the transit axis, and a central circular compass box, with a 3½-in. stepped ring graduated in degrees. The needle, of rectangular section with its longer side vertical, is provided with a lifting lever for clamping it. The vertical circle is attached to the telescope and transit axis, and is read by horizontal verniers on a standard. This bracket carries the clamp and tangent screw. The other standard carries a spirit level perpendicular to the transit axis. The telescope, fixed in the centre of the transit axis, has a rack-focussing objective of 1⋅5-in. aperture and 10-in. focal length, a fixed diaphragm having one vertical and three equidistant horizontal wires, and a slide-focussing Ramsden eyepiece. A sensitive spirit level is mounted parallel to the axis of the telescope.

interpretation: The introduction of the transit principle into medium and small-sized theodolites in England took place in the early part of the 19th century. This exhibit is an early example of such a theodolite.

description: In this instrument, made in the early part of the 19th century, the 8½-in. horizontal and the 7¼-in. vertical circles are graduated every 10′ and read by vernier to 10″. The vertical circle and telescope are rigidly joined to the transit axis and rotate with it, the verniers being fixed to one standard. The horizontal circle and vernier plate can rotate independently about the vertical axis, for repeating azimuth angles. The three footscrews for levelling the instrument are fixed to the base circle of a framed stand having a central conical socket, into which fits the hollow conical axis attached beneath the horizontal circle. The axis of the vernier plate fits within this and is kept in position by a screw and washer fitted in its lower end and abutting against the socket in the stand. The vernier plate carries three symmetrically placed vernier arms, with reading microscopes suspended above their verniers, and is provided with a sensitive spirit level, with its axis perpendicular to the transit axis. The standards supporting the transit axis project from the vernier plate, and have Y-s at their upper ends, one of which is adjustable. The axis is kept in position in these Y-s by metal straps; it is hollow, and permits the telescope to be illuminated by means of a lamp supported by a bracket fixed to one standard. The vernier bracket for reading the vertical circle carries a spirit level parallel to its two vernier arms, for setting their zeros. It has a projecting piece which fits between screws fixed to the standard, and keeps the verniers stationary when the telescope and circle rotate. The telescope has a fixed objective of 11-in. focal length and 1⋅8-in. clear aperture, and a central mirror for illuminating the axis at night. The eyepiece tube can be focussed by a rack and pinion mechanism, and carries the diaphragm, having five vertical and one horizontal threads, and the inverting, draw-focussing eye-piece, which fits in a slide permitting a slight lateral motion of the eyepiece. Clamps and tangent screws for fine motion are fitted to both circles and the horizontal vernier plate.

description: This is an early 19th-century example of a medium-sized transit theodolite. The 10-in. vertical and horizontal circles are graduated on silver every 10′ and read by two opposing verniers to 10″ of arc. The telescope transits at the eyepiece end, and its axis can be illuminated for night reading through the hollow horizontal axis of rotation. The instrument is mounted upon a tribrach having three footscrews for levelling; these rest upon a plate screwed to the tripod head and are kept in position by a locking plate of the Everest pattern. The horizontal circle can rotate freely about the vertical axis, or can be clamped to it and rotated slowly by means of a tangent screw. The vernier plate can be similarly clamped to the horizontal circle, or rotated freely. Reading microscopes are fixed on brackets above each vernier. An adjustable spirit level is fixed to the vernier plate, perpendicular to the line joining the two standards which support the vertical circle and telescope. The vertical circle is mounted upon the axis of rotation of the telescope, and is read by verniers at the ends of a bracket fixed to one standard. Reading microscopes are attached to this bracket for use with each vernier, and a spirit level is mounted in adjustable bearings on the bracket with its axis parallel to the line joining the vernier zeros. A tangent clamp and slow-motion screw connects the vertical circle to one standard. Upon the top of the telescope, parallel to its axis, is set a 5-in. trough compass. The lamp for illuminating the telescope axis rests upon a bracket fixed to one standard, with its lens opposite the end of the horizontal axis of rotation. A mirror in the centre of the telescope reflects the light down its axis.
