description: A highly compact transit theodolite, with vertical and horizontal circles of diameter 3.5 in., graduated in half-degrees and read by vernier to single minutes. It rests on three levelling screws, which can be fitted within three V-shaped notches in the top of the case. The horizontal circle is fixed to the tribrach, which carries a supplementary telescope, tangential to the circle, for keeping the back station in view. A single central standard projects vertically from the horizontal circle, and serves as an axis for the hollow cylinder which carries the vernier bracket for the horizontal axis at its lower extremity, and a bracket to which is fixed the vertical circle at its upper end. The telescope is fixed to an arm carrying opposing verniers for the vertical circle, and can rotate with this arm about a horizontal axis through the top of the standard. A spirit level is attached to the back of the vertical circle, at right angles to the standard. Tangent clamps and slow-motion screws are fixed to the vernier brackets of both circles, and there are magnifying lenses for facilitating the reading of the vernier. There are three verniers to the horizontal circle, symmetrically disposed round its circumference. The vertical circle has two verniers at opposite ends of a diameter. The main and supplementary telescopes are of equal size and power. Their objectives have a focal length of 3.5 in., and a clear aperture of 0.6 in. They slide in the telescope tubes for focussing. The eyepieces are of the Ramsden type. Diaphragms fitted with cross wires are fixed inside the telescope tubes. The one on the main telescope has two vertical wires and one horizontal wire. A diagonal eyepiece is provided for taking steep sights. As the telescope is slightly eccentric to the vertical standard, a counterpoise to balance its weight is fitted on the standard.

description: The horizontal circle in this instrument, which was made about 1875, has a separate axis with clamps and tangent screw for repeating angles, and is covered by a metal plate attached to the vernier plate. It has a diameter of 14 cm. and is graduated every 20' and read by opposing verniers and reading microscopes to 20". The reversible level fixed to the telescope has its upper and lower faces used before and after this is transited. The circular metal footplates attached to the extremities of the footscrews by ball and socket joints are peculiar to German instruments. They allow the theodolite to be moved over the surface of the tripod head for centring, which movement is permitted by the special arrangement for connecting the instrument and tripod. The vertical circle has a diameter of 12 cm. and is graduated in half-degrees and read by a single vernier to minutes. It is rigidly fixed to the transit axis and telescope. This has a fixed objective of 22-cm. focal length and 3-cm. aperture, and a rack-focussing eyepiece tube, carrying the fixed diaphragm and a slide-focussing inverting eyepiece. The reversible level is attached by adjustable screws parallel to the axis of the telescope. Any error in adjustment between the level and telescope is automatically corrected by transiting the telescope and again levelling it after rotation horizontally through 180°. An axis clamp and tangent screw for fine vertical motion is attached to one standard, the V-bearing or the axis being adjustably vertically. The axis is kept in the bearings by metal straps. Between the standards is a small circular spirit level, for roughly setting the plate horizontal, the final levelling being tested by the spirit level attached to the telescope. The vernier plate has a clamp and tangent screw in addition to that on the horizontal circle. The instrument has a tribrach mounting, with three levelling screws, and is connected to the tripod head by a central screw and spring. On loosening this the theodolite can be moved laterally for centring above the station point.

description: This is a repeating theodolite, made about 1875, and resembles the adjacent one by Fennel in general construction. It differs, however, in having an ordinary one-sided spirit level attached to the telescope, which has also a Huygens, not a Ramsden, eyepiece. The horizontal circle has a diameter of 14 cm., is graduated every 20' and read by two opposing verniers and reading microscopes to 30". The vertical circle, of 10.5 cm. diam., is divided to 30' and read by opposing verniers to single minutes. The telescope has a fixed objective, of 2.5 cm. clear aperture and with the field lens of the eyepiece, a focal length of 23 cm. The eyepiece is focussed by a rack and pinion arrangement, the cross-wire diaphragm being fixed between the two lenses. The telescope, rigidly attached to the horizontal axis and the vertical circle, transits at the eyepiece end, and has a sensitive longitudinal spirit level mounted on it in adjustable bearings. The vertical vernier bracket is screwed to one standard, whilst the other carries the tangent screw and clamping spring for the transit axis. The horizontal vernier plate carries a metal cover which protects the horizontal circle and supports a central circular spirit level, and the reading microscopes. There are windows in this plate above the verniers, and reflectors are attached to the microscopes for illuminating the field. The horizontal circle has a separate axis, with clamp and tangent screw for repetition. This fits in the socket fixed to the tribrach, which has three levelling screws furnished at their feet with small metal plates, to which they are connected by ball and socket joints. The instrument is connected to its tripod by the usual German central screw, with a flange and opposing spring which fix the instrument tightly, but on loosening the screw permit the theodolite to be displaced laterally for accurate centring over the station point.

The vernier plate has an axis clamp and tangent screw, and carries a central socket in which the vertical axis rotates. A horizontal bracket fixed across the top of this socket carries the bearings for the transit axis. Both bearings can be adjusted on the bracket, and tested for horizontality by a sensitive striding level. The transit axis has a clamp and slow-motion screw to fix it to the vertical socket. description: This instrument was made at the end of the 19th century and used in the British Antarctic Expedition, 1901. It has 7-in. vertical and horizontal circles, graduated every 10' and reading by two opposing verniers and reading microscopes to 10". All adjustable screws and parts are covered with wash leather to protect the operator's fingers from frost. The horizontal and alidade circles are enclosed in a metal case, the verniers being covered by hinged plates. Clamps and tangent screws are fitted to both circles, and to the vertical circle, which is not covered, and is fixed to the transit axis. The vertical vernier bracket is clamped to a lug on one standard by opposing screws, and carries a sensitive spirit level perpendicular to the transit axis. The transit axis rests in Y-bearings on the standards, one trunnion being adjustable vertically, and is kept in position by metal retaining straps; it is hollow and has a lens at one end for illuminating the telescope axis. The telescope is rigidly fixed to this axis and transits at the eyepiece end only. It has an objective of 11-in. focal length and 1·5-in. aperture, focussed by a rack and pinion mechanism controlled from the eyepiece end. The diaphragm has one vertical and one horizontal thread, both adjustable laterally. Three slide focussing eyepieces are provided, one inverting, one diagonal, and one erecting. There is a central reflector in the telescope for illuminating its axis by light coming through the transit axis from a lamp fixed to one standard. A striding level is provided for testing the transit axis. The vernier cover plate carries a spirit level, with its axis parallel to the transit axis, whilst a perpendicular level is fixed to one standard. A central compass with a 4-in. ring graduated in degrees is attached to the vernier plate. The instrument has a tribrach mounting with three levelling footscrews, whose points rest in a trivet plate; this is provided with a locking plate of the Everest type attached to the tripod head.

description: This is a compact theodolite specially designed for Alpine and military surveying. It has 3-in. vertical and horizontal circles, divided to half-degrees and read by verniers to single minutes. A diagonal eyepiece is provided for astronomical observations of stars near the zenith. The construction of the instrument is similar to that of a modern vernier theodolite of twice the size. The transit axis rests on standards projecting from the vernier plate, and carries a central telescope and the vertical circle fixed to it. The vernier arm projects from one standard, and a tangent clamp and slow-motion screw is fitted to the other, which also carries a spirit level perpendicular to the transit axis. A similar level parallel to the transit axis is fixed on the vernier plate, which also carries a central compass box, having a 1-in. ring divided in degrees. The compass needle is provided with a lifting lever for clamping it when desired. The vernier plate rotates independently about the vertical axis and has a clamp and tangent screw for connecting it to the horizontal circle, which has a similar clamp and tangent screw connecting it to the tribrach. This latter has three footscrews, with their feet clamped in a trivet plate by a locking plate of the Everest type. The trivet plate can be screwed to the tripod head. The telescope has a rack-focussing objective of 4·5-in. focal length and 0·65-in. aperture, a fixed cross-wire diaphragm and a set of slide-focussing eyepieces, one erecting, one inverting, and one diagonal. A reflector for illuminating the cross wires at night is fitted in front of the objective.

description: A 17th-century instrument for measuring angles in either a vertical or a horizontal plane. It consists of a wooden rectangular frame to which can be screwed a brass socket in either of two positions for setting the plane of the rectangle horizontal or vertical. Two adjacent sides of the rectangle have folding brass sights at their corners for setting off right angles. A movable brass index arm, provided with folding sights, is centred on one of the sighted sides of the rectangle and rotates over a brass scale mounted on the other side. This scale is graduated to read tangents, to the nearest tenth. A clamp and screw fixed to the index arm serve to clamp it in any desired position to a brass arc fixed to the rectangle. The outer sight on the arm carries a plumb-line when the rectangle is horizontal. When vertical angles are being measured, the plumb-line is detached and fixed to a screw so that it hangs parallel to the brass scale in the plane of the rectangle.
interpretation: Instrument for measuring angles in either a vertical or a horizontal plane. The scale is graduated to read tangents, to the nearest tenth.

description: The Dip-Sector was first designed and made by Troughton for measuring the "dip of the horizon" from an elevated observing point. The graduated sector, index arm, index mirror and horizon mirror are the same as in the sextant, but the telescope has its eyepiece at right angles to its objective, a reflecting mirror being interposed between the two. This enables the observer to measure the zenith angle between the apparent horizon lines to his left and right. By rotating the handle through a half turn, he can measure the corresponding nadir angle. The quarter of the difference between these two readings is the required dip angle between his apparent and true horizons. The index error is eliminated in this method. The horizon mirror, fixed to the sector, is partly silvered and partly unsilvered. The index glass, which rotates with the index arm, is wholly silvered, and has a central index. The arm carries the vernier, and can be clamped to the sector at any point, further rotation being effected by a tangent screw. The telescope can be adjusted to vary its lateral distance from the sector by a screw, and the handle can be rotated and clamped in any position parallel to the face of the sector.

description: Three types of microscope for reading the circles of small theodolites. In each case, the circles are completely enclosed in metal, dust-proof cases, and the microscopes are consequently provided with mirror reflecting tubes for illuminating the graduations. The first microscope is a "Schätz" or "Estimation" Microscope, and has a single fixed line marked in its focal plane, parallel to the graduations of the circle. It is used in theodolites having 10-cm. circles, graduated every 10'. The position of the fixed microscope line between these graduations is estimated to a single minute. The second microscope, known as a "Nonien-Mikroskop," has a fixed vernier scale marked in its focal plane, and is used for theodolites having 13-cm. circles graduated to 5'. Ten divisions of the vernier scale correspond to nine of the circle, whence the position of the zero vernier line can be read to 30", or even to 15" by estimation. Alternate graduations of the vernier scale are numbered consecutively from 0 to 5, and represent minutes. The third microscope, designated a "Skalen-Mikroskop," is of the type devised by Hensoldt in 1870, and is used on theodolites having 13·5-cm. circles, graduated in 20'. A fixed scale in the focal plane of the microscope has ten divisions, numbered right to left, exactly covering the interval between consecutive graduations of the circle. The position of one circle graduation on this scale can be read to one-tenth of a scale division, i.e., to 12". In this and the second microscope, the reading edges of the two scales slightly overlap each other, which ensures a sharper reading.

In each case, the circles are completely enclosed in metal, dust-proof cases, and the microscopes are consequently provided with mirror reflecting tubes for illuminating the graduations. Used for estimating to a single minute, reading to 30" or 15" by estimation, and reading to one-tenth of a scale division, i.e., to 12".

description: A tripod head fitted with a "shifting centre" arrangement, permitting the centre of the attached theodolite to be displaced any distance up to about 1 in. in any direction without removing the theodolite from the tripod or altering the position of this latter. A small circular spirit level is embedded in the top of the tripod plate and is used to set this approximately level.

description: A 2-ft. transit theodolite. This instrument was made at the commencement of the Irish survey and was first used in 1828 for checking the measurement of the Lough Foyle base by triangulation. It was further employed between 1829 and 1862 in measuring the main angles of the Principal Triangulation of Great Britain and Ireland. This theodolite differs from the adjacent 3-ft. one made by Ramsden in that its telescope can transit completely between the supporting pillars, and the horizontal circle is mounted upon a repeating stage so that both circle and microscopes can be independently rotated. The horizontal circle is 2 ft. in diam., and is divided on silver to 5′ and read by five microscopes to 1″. Two vertical circles of 12-in. diam. are fixed to the telescope; they are divided to 5′ and read by single microscopes to 2″. The telescope has a fixed objective of 27-in. focal length and 2·1-in. aperture, and a rack-focussing eyepiece tube carrying the diaphragm and erecting eyepiece. The diaphragm has one fixed horizontal wires, with five equidistant vertical wires moved laterally by a micrometer screw. The repeating stage rests by means of three footscrews upon an iron triangle fixed upon the head of the wooden tripod stand. It has an upper rotating tribrach supporting the horizontal circle and upper axis of the theodolite. The five microscopes reading this circle rotate with the telescope and upper part about this axis. Clamps and tangent screws are fitted to both circles and the repeating stage, and four spirit levels are provided for adjusting the telescope and horizontal axis of rotation.

description: The example shown was made in 1884, and the probable error of a single observation made with it was about one second of arc. divided on silver to 10' and read by opposing verniers and reading microscopes to 10". The arcs are fixed to the axis of rotation carrying the telescope and counterpoise, whilst the verniers are clamped to one standard. The telescope has a rack-focussing objective of 2.5-in. aperture and 20-in. focal length, a fixed star diaphragm, and a slide-focussing Ramsden eyepiece.
interpretation: Theodolites of this type were used by the Ordnance Survey in the Secondary Triangulation of the United Kingdom during the latter half of the 19th century.

description: A zenith sector designed by Sir George Airy and constructed under his direction. It was used between 1842 and 1850 for determining the latitudes of twenty-seven stations of the Principal Triangulation. The telescope is pivoted horizontally to a revolving gunmetal frame which is itself pivoted vertically in a fixed cast-iron framework. The latter is supported upon a rectangular plate which in turn rests upon a cast-iron trough; this trough was usually screwed upon heavy wooden pickets driven into the ground. Four micrometer microscopes attached to the telescope serve to read its inclination to the zenith upon two graduated arcs, mounted upon the revolving frame. Each arc extends over 45° of a circle of radius 20.5 in., and is divided to 5' and read by the microscopes to one-quarter of a second. The telescope has an objective of aperture 3.7 in. and 46 in. focal length, a micrometer diaphragm with five fixed and one movable wires, and an inverting eyepiece of magnification 70. Three sensitive spirit levels are fixed in adjustable bearings across the back of the revolving frame. In taking observations of a star's transit, the frame is quickly rotated to permit face east and face west readings of the telescope. The probable error of a single observation of latitude with this instrument was about 1".
interpretation: Used for determining latitudes in the Principal Triangulation of Great Britain and Ireland. Designed to replace Ramsden's zenith sector after its destruction by fire. Used for determining the latitudes of twenty-seven stations of the Principal Triangulation.
interpretation_source: "Astronomical Observations made with Airy's Zenith Sector," Ordnance Survey

description: This portable sector was made at the beginning of the 19th century for use in America and was afterwards transferred to Copenhagen. The main telescope for observing stars near the zenith is pivoted horizontally near its objective end to the top of a vertical hollow brass cylinder, which carries at its lower end the fixed graduated sector over which the eyepiece of the telescope rotates. Two micrometer microscopes fixed to the telescope serve to read its inclination to the vertical upon separate scales engraved on the sector. The scales, each of which covers about 15° and is divided to 3', start at opposite ends of the sector and overlap about 5° in the centre. A third scale, continuous across the whole sector, is read by an index and serves as a check. The telescope has an objective of 2.5-in. aperture and 45-in. focal length. Its motion over the sector is controlled by a clamp and tangent screw. The base of the vertical cylinder is connected to a horizontal circle by six vertical pillars and can rotate with this circle about a vertical axis coincident with the cylinder axis. A long plummet suspended within the cylinder along its axis rests in a water vessel, inside the pillars, and serves to set the axis vertical. Its position is observed by two perpendicular microscopes fixed in the cylinder below the graduated sector. A small telescope pivoted to the cylinder is used to observe circumpolar stars for setting the sector in the meridian. The three levelling foot screws of the tribrach rest on the top plate of a strong mahogany tripod. A small spirit level is mounted on the cylinder for rough levelling, and an adjustable counterpoise balances the telescope.
interpretation: Used for observing stars near the zenith, setting the sector in the meridian, and setting the axis vertical.

description: The zenith sector represented in these two photographs was designed by Lt.-Col. A. Strange and constructed by Troughton and Simms in 1869 for use in the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. By means of this and a somewhat improved instrument of similar design and make, many latitudes were determined in India during the period 1884-1900; from 1890, however, a more convenient zenith telescope has been mostly employed in India for determining latitudes by Talcott's method. The instrument illustrated consists of a telescope of 4-in. aperture and 48-in. focal length, mounted rigidly upon a double sector which forms part of a graduated vertical circle of 3 ft. diam. The telescope can rotate upon a horizontal axis supported by a vertical metal pillar, and the vertical rotation is measured by means of four microscopes fixed to the frame carrying the axis. The instrument can be accurately adjusted upon its base frame so that the vertical sector revolves in the meridian plane, and its zero line is adjusted to be horizontal by means of a sensitive spirit level; the zero line is perpendicular to the telescope axis of sight, which therefore points to the zenith when the former is horizontal. The sector is graduated on silver every 5'; each limb extends over 55° and is read by two microscopes, separated 20" from each other, to single seconds; a separate smaller microscope serves to read degrees and minutes on the sector graduations. The telescope has a micrometer eyepiece fitted with a diagonal reflecting prism. A setting circle, of diameter 8 in., divided to 10' and read by vernier to 10", is mounted on the telescope near its eyepiece, and is provided with a small level and also a very sensitive one, which latter permits the instrument to be used as a zenith telescope for observations by Talcott's method.

description: A photograph illustrating a 3-in. portable zenith telescope for determining latitudes by the Talcott method. The original instrument was supplied to the Survey of India in 1909, and is a typical example of the modern zenith instrument for geodetic work. The telescope, of 3-in. aperture and about 42-in. focal length, is mounted at one end of the horizontal axis by means of a centrepiece, which also carries the Talcott level frame. The latter has two chambered levels, running 0·1 in. to 2" of arc, enclosed in special sealed cases lined with thermal insulating material, and is provided with a long sensitive clamp and slow motion screw permitting an accurate adjustment in altitude. The horizontal axis has a weight relieving spring and ball race at the telescope end and a counterpoise at the other end; it is hollow to permit illumination of the telescope field by means of an oil or electric lamp. The telescope has a steel micrometer eyepiece, giving a value of about 30" to one revolution of the micrometer screw. A 7-in. setting circle, divided on silver to 30' and reading by vernier to 1', is mounted on the telescope near the eyepiece end. A 10 in. diam. horizontal circle, divided on silver to 30' and read by vernier to 1', is mounted on the tribrach base, which is provided with three levelling foot-screws. A clamp and slow motion screw controls the vertical axis motion, and two adjustable stops are provided to enable the telescope to be rapidly rotated in azimuth through 180°. A striding level is mounted above the horizontal axis of the instrument.

description: A transit of this type was used about 1850 by F. G. Struve in his measurement of an arc of the 52nd parallel from Haverfordwest to Eastern Russia. The telescope has a 2·7 in. objective and is "broken" where it meets the hollow transit axis, a diagonal prism being here interposed to deflect the light into the eyepiece tube at one end of this axis. The diaphragm of the Ramsden eyepiece, which has a pair of movable wires actuated by a micrometer screw in addition to an adjustable reticule, is illuminated by a lamp mounted at the other end of the transit axis. A vertical circle of 11 in. diam., divided on silver to 10', is fixed to the transit axis near the eyepiece, and is read by an index on the adjacent standard. The steel pivots of the transit axis rest on high standards projecting from the levelling platform, which is supported on the wooden tripod stand by three levelling screws, having a point, line and plane contact respectively with the bearing plates. Two small bubble-levels are used to set the base horizontal by means of the foot-screws, and the transit axis is finally adjusted horizontal by a sensitive hanging level. The telescope can be lifted from its bearings on the standards and reversed end for end by means of a rotating framework mounted inside the levelling platform and carrying two extending forks which support the transit axis during the rotation.
interpretation: Used for measurement of an arc of the 52nd parallel. The telescope is "broken" where it meets the hollow transit axis, a diagonal prism being here interposed to deflect the light into the eyepiece tube at one end of this axis.

description: A transit instrument with a telescope of 3-in. aperture and about 30-in. focal length, having two setting circles of 6 in. diam., reading by verniers to 20", mounted near its eyepiece end. The telescope is mounted upon a rigid horizontal axis fitted with a long clamp and slow-motion screw. The axis rests in bearings upon a massive U-shaped frame which permits the telescope to transit, and also carries a mechanism for lifting the telescope axis from its pivots and reversing it through 180° in azimuth. The supporting frame is adjustably mounted upon a base plate which can be fixed on a masonry pier. The diaphragm of the telescope is of glass and has seven lines; it is illuminated through the transit axis by means of an electric lamp at one end of the latter. A sensitive striding level is mounted above the axis. Levels, tangent and slow motion screws are fitted to both setting circles.
interpretation: Transit instruments of the type here illustrated are sufficiently portable to be used for time and longitude observations in geodetic surveys. Transits very similar to the original of this photograph have been supplied to the Colonies in recent years.

description: This instrument, also known as a "Prismatic Astrolabe," was designed by MM. Claude and Driencourt about the year 1900, and is used for the astronomical determination of latitude, local time and azimuth. It acts on the principle of determining the exact moment at which a known star crosses a horizontal circle of constant angle, namely 60°. The instrument exhibited is the "geodetic" model of the firm, and has a telescope of aperture 40 mm. and magnification 75 diam. Latitudes can be determined with it to 0.4" and time to 0.04/sin \lambda sec., where \lambda is the co-latitude of the observing station. The telescope can rotate in azimuth upon one end of a horizontal plate, which carries a mercury artificial horizon at its other end and can itself rotate above the graduated horizontal circle of the instrument. This circle is divided in degrees, serving any particular star. An equilateral glass prism of sides and height 45 mm. is mounted in front of the objective lens of the telescope, with its base vertical and apex edge horizontal. When the star is nearly at an altitude of 60°, two images are seen of it in the telescope, one by light refracted through the prism and telescope, and the other by light reflected from the mercury horizon before refraction in the prism. At the precise moment that the star crosses the 60° horizontal circle, the two images meet on the same horizontal line of the telescope graticule. By a series of similar observations of the times of crossing of known stars, both latitude and local time can be ascertained from tables.
interpretation: Used for the astronomical determination of latitude, local time and azimuth. It acts on the principle of determining the exact moment at which a known star crosses a horizontal circle of constant angle, namely 60°. Latitudes can be determined with it to 0.4" and time to 0.04/sin \lambda sec., where \lambda is the co-latitude of the observing station. By a series of similar observations of the times of crossing of known stars, both latitude and local time can be ascertained from tables.
interpretation_source: Plate VII, Fig. 1, p. 90. "Handbook of the Prismatic Astrolabe," by J. Ball and H. Knox-Shaw, 1919.

description: A surveying instrument in which the vertical semicircle is fixed to the alidade with its curved edge upwards, and the telescope rotates tangentially upon it. This arrangement permits nearly vertical sights to be taken and renders the instrument suitable for mine surveying. The vertical arc and telescope can easily be detached from the alidade for packing the instrument. The alidade also carries a compass box. The telescope has a simple inverting eyepiece with a cross-thread diaphragm. There is no focussing arrangement. A spirit level is mounted in adjustable bearings beneath the telescope.

description: The plain mine surveyor's dial is very similar to the old circumferentor and has been much employed in England owing to its adaptability to surveying in low galleries and suitability for traversing. The instrument exhibited is a mid-19th-century dial, with a 5-in. compass ring graduated in degrees and a vernier fixed to the movable alidade reading to 3'. The compass ring and base are mounted upon an axial socket perpendicular to their planes and can be rotated about the central axis which fits in this socket and terminates in a spherical ball. This latter is gripped by another socket and can be clamped in any desired position so that the plane of the compass faces any direction. A slit in the socket allows the compass to take up a vertical position for measuring altitude angles. When measuring azimuth angles, the plane of the compass is levelled by means of a pair of perpendicular tube spirit levels fixed to the alidade. This is attached to the compass case, and carries combined back-sights and foresights at each end. The alidade and compass case, with the internal vernier scale, can be rotated independently of the compass ring and angles measured as in a theodolite, or the case can be clamped to the compass ring and the two rotated together about the axis of the latter for taking magnetic bearings, as in the ordinary compass. In the former case, the alidade is fitted with a tangent screw for slow-motion adjustment. The sights are 6 in. high and fixed at a distance of 1 ft. apart on the alidade. Each sight has both a slit and a pin-hole backsight and a long single-wire and a cross-wire foresight. The aperture and cross-wire sights are for use in measuring altitude angles. For this purpose the compass needle is locked by operating the lifting lever, the plane of the compass is set vertical, and the lid is placed in position on the box, and a plumb-line suspended from a stud in this lid. The opposite edge of the lid is graduated in degrees up to 45° each way and has a scale of hypotenusal increments engraved on it.

description: The chief feature of this mining dial, which is a modern example of the type invented by John Hedley in 1830, is the use of a rocking circle, pivoted externally to the compass box, to carry either plain sights or a telescope. This arrangement permits a fairly steep vertical angle to be measured, the angle being read by an index revolving with the rocking circle over a graduated semicircle fixed to the compass box. The compass ring can rotate inside the box about the vertical axis, for measuring azimuth angles independently of the needle, or can be clamped to the box for taking magnetic bearings.
interpretation: A modern example of a mining dial invented by John Hedley in 1830. Its features allow for the measurement of steep vertical angles and both azimuth angles and magnetic bearings.

description: A sextant of the usual type employed in marine surveying. It has a graduated arc of 8-in. radius, divided on silver to 10' and read by vernier and magnifier to 10". The arc extends from 0° to 150°, each numbered degree being really only half a degree. The vernier moves with the index arm, which is pivoted at the centre of the arc and carries the index mirror. A long telescope is mounted in the usual up and down piece on one outer radius of the arc and faces the horizon mirror, mounted on the other outer radius. Coloured glasses are provided for astronomical sights, and a handgrip is mounted on the under side of the frame.
interpretation: Employed in marine surveying.

interpretation: This sextant is believed to have belonged to the German surveying ship "Moewe." It is of the usual construction and has an arc of radius 20 cm., divided to 30' and read by vernier to 1'. The index arm, carrying the index mirror at its centre and the vernier at its extremity, is provided with a clamp and tangent screw for slow motion. Coloured glasses are fitted on pivots near both mirrors. A handgrip fixed beneath the frame is used when taking vertical angles, and has a screw socket beneath it for attaching a perpendicular handgrip used for taking horizontal angles. The telescope has two erecting eyepieces, of magnification 3 and 4 diam. respectively. A plain sight tube is also provided. The telescope supporting ring can be elevated or depressed by a fine screw in the usual manner.

description: This instrument, which was salved from a German warship sunk at Scapa, has a complete graduated circle instead of a sextant, and a totally reflecting right-angled prism instead of the usual horizon mirror; it is of the type first made by Pistor and Martins in 1845. The substitution of the prism for the horizon mirror enables angles up to 180° to be taken and also gives a clearer image at extreme angles, whilst the use of a complete circle and an index arm fitted with two opposing verniers, minimizes errors due to inequalities of graduation or inaccuracy in centring the index mirror and arm. The circle has a diameter of 13 cm. and is graduated to 10', corresponding to 20' of the angle measured. This angle is read by the vernier to 20". Only part of the graduations, namely, those under one vernier, are numbered and in these a gap is left where the telescope and head of the observer foul the line of sight of the index mirror. This latter has its plane inclined at about 20° to the zeros of the index arm to which it is attached. The horizon prism is mounted with its reflecting face parallel to the index mirror when the verniers are at zero. It is opposite the lower half of the telescope, which is mounted in the usual " up and down " piece, the upper half of the field being left free from direct vision. The index arm has the usual clamp and tangent screw at one extremity, and a wooden handgrip for holding the instrument is attached beneath the circle. A reading microscope is fixed to a rotating bracket for magnifying the scales, and a set of smoked glasses for varying the illumination of the telescope field is attached to a rotating pivot near the supporting ring.
interpretation: The substitution of the prism for the horizon mirror enables angles up to 180° to be taken and also gives a clearer image at extreme angles, whilst the use of a complete circle and an index arm fitted with two opposing verniers, minimizes errors due to inequalities of graduation or inaccuracy in centring the index mirror and arm.

description: This type of station keeper is essentially similar in construction to a box sextant, having a graduated arc of 6-in. radius extending over 20°. By measuring on this arc the angle subtended at his position by a fixed length on the distant object, the observer can calculate his distance from that object, or, having calculated the necessary angle, can set it on the instrument and keep his distance constant. The instrument consists of a sector-shaped box having its wider end open and its narrower end closed, save for a pin-hole aperture for sighting. At the open end, within the box, is mounted a fixed "horizon" mirror, whilst a movable index mirror is pivoted near the closed end and geared to an external rotating index arm, which moves over a graduated arc on the upper face of the box. The gearing is done by rack and pinion gear, which causes the index arm to rotate through twice the angle through which the index mirror moves. The arc is graduated in half-degrees from 0° to 20° and the index arm carries a vernier reading to 5′. In using the instrument the observer sights one end of the distant base directly through the space below the horizon mirror, and the other end by double reflection at the two mirrors, and moves his position or the index arm until the two ends appear coincident.
interpretation: By measuring on this arc the angle subtended at his position by a fixed length on the distant object, the observer can calculate his distance from that object, or, having calculated the necessary angle, can set it on the instrument and keep his distance constant.

description: The arms of a station pointer are often fitted with sights which permit the instrument to act as a theodolite and thus to measure the angles subtended by three known points at the observing station. On detaching the arm piece from the circle and applying it to the chart like an ordinary station pointer, the position of the observing station can be plotted. The instrument exhibited is of this combination type, and was salved from a German warship sunk at Scapa Flow. It has a graduated circle of 11-in. diam., with its edge divided on German silver to single degrees. This circular plate can rotate within a hollow central axis which terminates below in a spherical ball; this ball forms part of a ball and socket joint connecting the instrument to a stand. The plate can thus be set in any plane and clamped by means of a threaded collar acting on the joint; it can then be rotated in this plane and clamped by a radial screw threaded in its outer axis and impinging on its inner one. The arms of the instrument are mounted on a separate circular ring which has a central pin fitting within a hole in the centre of the plate. Each arm is pivoted round this pin and can be turned about it and clamped to the edge of the circular ring when the arm is directed towards the corresponding fixed point. The central pin acts as backsight for the observation, whilst each arm has a folding slit foresight fixed at its outer end. The subtended angles can then be read off on the graduated circle if required and the arm piece removed and applied to the chart. The bevelled edges of the arms are then made to pass through the corresponding fixed points on the chart, when the central pin marks the position of the observing station. This pin is mounted loosely in the arm piece and its point kept slightly above the plane of the arms by a spring. On depressing the head of the pin, its point makes an indentation in the chart and thus plots the position of the observing station.
interpretation: Used to measure the angles subtended by three known points at the observing station, allowing plotting of the observing station's position. The instrument can act as a theodolite. The position of the observing station can be plotted by applying the arm piece to a chart.

description: A modified form of sextant designed by T. Nordenfelt about 1884 for rangefinding at sea. Observations are taken with the plane of the sextant vertical from a point on board ship at a known height above sea level upon the water line of a distant object and simultaneously upon the horizon. When the horizon and water line images are made to coincide by revolving the index arm, the reading of the index on the graduated arc gives the range of the distant object directly. The index mirror is not mounted upon the pivot of the rotating arm, but upon an eccentric pivot, connected to the arm by a cam and pin mechanism, which causes the mirror to rotate through a much smaller angle than the arm; this enables the angle swept out by the reflected ray to be varied very gradually between narrow limits, whilst the index traverses an arc of 60° or thereabouts. As the angle of depression of the distant object below the horizon varies inversely as the range, if the base—i.e. the height of the observer above sea level—is constant, the arc of the sextant can be graduated to read the range directly. Different arcs are, however, necessary for different observing heights, and three are provided, two for heights of 96 ft. and the third for a height of 47 ft. ; any arc can be fixed in the sextant frame by means of clamping pins. The effect of the dip of the horizon is allowed for on the graduated arcs. The rotating arm is provided with one fixed index mark and another index which can be displaced relative to the fixed one by means of a tangent screw; the arm has a separate clamp and tangent screw. Two telescopes, of different fields and magnifications, are provided.
interpretation: Modified form of sextant designed for rangefinding at sea. The instrument directly reads the range of a distant object based on the angle of depression from a known height. Different graduated arcs are provided for different observing heights.

description: This instrument was designed for photographic surveying. It consists of an accurately adjustable camera of nearly constant focus, fixed to the vernier plate of a 6 in. theodolite which gives the azimuth angle of the optical axis of the camera to 30", and is provided with an ordinary parallel plate four levelling screw mounting for attachment to the tripod. The camera box, which is made of teak, has a pair of perpendicular spirit levels and a 2-in. compass box attached to its top. The front consists of a brass plate mounted in horizontal and vertical slides, and adjusted in both directions by means of fine screws. It carries a centrally mounted Zeiss extreme angle (about 130°) anastigmat lens of 141-mm. focal length. The vertical and horizontal position of the lens is measurable by scales and verniers to 0.04 mm. The back of the camera can slide in the box and is moved by a twin rack and pinion arrangement, actuated by thumb wheels at each side. The focal length of the camera for any position of the back is read by a scale and vernier to 0.04 mm. The ground glass is graduated in centimetre squares, the central vertical and horizontal lines having millimetre graduations. Four triangular brass teeth are fixed in the centres of the edges of the back, and press against the front face of the plate during exposure. Their images on the plate after exposure serve to determine the horizon line and principal vertical line of the picture. The slides, twelve in number, are "single," and must be changed after each exposure. The base of the camera box has guides and screw threads for fixing it to the vernier plate of the theodolite, so that the principal point of the lens is vertically above the centre of the horizontal circle. This latter is graduated in half-degrees and read by opposing verniers to 30". Clamps and tangent screws for fine motion are fitted to both vernier plate and horizontal circle. The instrument is levelled by means of the spirit level on top of the camera box, and the four footscrews.
